speechtext: Mr. M. STEELE (South Perth) moved, that the Bills reported this day by the Select Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills be placed on the Order Paper for consideration by Committee of the Whole this day.

Mr. Speaker,
I think both Houses should be made aware of these Bills. The other day a similar motion was passed, and afterwards about twenty-five Bills were presented, including divorce and other private Bills, of which we knew absolutely nothing, the Bills not having been printed and distributed. I do not think it is fair to pass legislation in this way. I might state, further, that such a motion requires the unanimous consent of the House.

It does not protect
the rights of the people.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Rule 40, which is the
rule governing notice, specifically exempts Private Bills; and my information is that it has been the invariable practice of the House to interpret this rule as requiring no notice of motion in respect to Private Bills. That being so, in my judgment the motion is in order. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?
Motion agreed to.

On page 4011 of unrevised Hansard of May 25, in the vote on the Bill for the Manufacture of Oleomargarine, I find my name among those voting for the amendment, which is quite correct. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the announcement that the work of the census enumerators is to begin on the first day of June, I beg leave to direct the attention of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) to information I have received that, although about one-third of the population in the city and one-half of the population of the county of Moncton are French speaking, the enumerators appointed-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I want to ask a question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Even so, the hon. member could hardly do that on the Orders of the Day. Apparently the enumerators have been appointed, and the hon. member is in effect calling attention to an omission on the part of the Government, which he could not do at this stage.
No, Mr. Speaker, I want to know if my information is correct that the census enumerators appointed in that section are not French-speaking gentlemen.

My attention was called to this by the Prime Minister and I referred the question to the Dominion Statistician. I have not yet received word from him. My impression is that enumerators have already been appointed and have been under instruction.
I have always thought it was only right that amongst the enumerators in French settlements of English-speaking counties, there should be gentlemen who understood the French language.
Otherwise it is impossible to carry on the work in some sections.
On the Orders of the Day:

I would like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question which, even without formal notice on the Order Paper, pos-
sibly he might answer to-morrow. What salaries are being paid to members of the Royal Commission now conducting an inquiry into the grain business in the western provinces; also what are the names of the secretaries, reporters and staff employed, together with their salaries.

speakeroldname: Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) :
speechtext: I will give my hon. friend a complete answer to the question to-morrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Senate having insisted upon the amendments which they made to this Bill and in which this House declined to concur, and there being reason to hope that a conference on the subject might lead to an agreement, I beg to move:
That a message be sent to the Senate respectfully requesting a free conference with Their Honours to consider certain amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 60, intituled: "An Act to amend the Judges Act," to which amendments this House has not agreed and upon which the Senate insist, and any amendment which at such conference it may be considered desirable to make to the said Bill or amendments thereto.
Motion agreed to.

On the Order:
Second reading of Bill No. 201, to amend the) Penitentiary Act.-The Minister of Justice.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The House will recall that
when this Bill was introduced the suggestion was made that certain of its provisions perhaps called for more mature consideration than it would be possible to give them at the present time. I have attached to that representation the weight to which it seemed to be entitled, and I have gone over the existing legislation. As it appears that the principal or more important matters covered by this Bill can be dealt with in a certain measure without legislation, and as, therefore, the plans in mind can be initiated without this legislation, in accordance with the suggestion made I beg to move that the order for this Bill be discharged.
Motion agreed to.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Public Works-harbours and rivers-Ontario, $370,850.

I move that the
appropriation be considered item by item.

Motion agreed to.
Collingwood'-breakwater reconstruction, $25,000.

What is the explanation
of this item?

This revote is required for the completion of a contract with the York Construction Company for the reconstruction of 750 feet of the superstructure at the outer end of the eastern breakwater, in reinforced concrete. The estimated cost was $50,000. Last year $25,000 was expended ; accordingly the amount required to complete is $25,000.

Will that complete the
work?
Mr. McCurdy: Yes.
In what riding is Collingwood?
North Simcoe.

Item agreed to.
Depot Harbour-repairs and renewals tc wharves, $15,000.
Last year the appropriation amounted to $36,000. Did that cover repairs also, and were the repairs done under contract?
The work is under contract. This amount is required to complete the construction.

What county is that
in?
Parry Sound.

Item agreed to.
Kingston-maintenance and operation ot combined wharves and bridges, $17,900.
What is the explanation of this item?

This amount is for
maintenance and operation of the combined roadway, wharves and bridges over the Cataraqui river at Kingston.

Was the amount of $12,800
voted last year, spent?
Yes.

Is this a continuation of
the works, or repairs? Or what is it?

The appropriation
asked for this year is for replanking and repainting the bridges. Many public works are in such condition that they call for continuous and extensive repairs, and it is sometimes difficult to tell exactly where to draw the line. Last year, as I have said, the amount of $12,800 was expended towards keeping this work in some sort of decent repair, and the amount asked for this year is absolutely necessary.

What proportion of this
appropriation is to be expended on the road?

Details of last year's
expenditures are as follows:
Power for this work	$1,400
Light	 700
Oils and gasoline	 350
Globes, lamps, fuses, etc	 350
Road maintenance and new roadway
surface	 1	 2,000
Replanking bridges	 4,500
Repainting bridges	 3,500
How is it that the Dominion Government have to maintain a roadway at Kingston?

Anyone who has been there and remembers the roadway across to the Royal Military College will

understand. It is a causeway across the water; it had to be built and made permanent. It is not a road in the city or anything of that nature; it connects across to the Royal Military College.
Is the road on Government property?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Owen Sound-wharf reconstruction, $70,000.
How much was spent on that last year?
The contract was let last year, but no progress was made with the work. The contractor has assembled the materials and is now ready to proceed.

What was the contract
price?
There were five tenders received, the lowest being that of E. Conroy, for $89,768.40. The others ran up to as high as $143,000.
Has anything been paid out on the contract yet?
No.
The contract is for $89,000 and you are asking for a vote of only $70,000.
The vote we are asking will pretty well cover the work that will be done this year. The contract will hardly be finished by this time next year.
What constituency is this in?
North Grey.

Item agreed to.
Port Colborne - repairs to breakwaters. $55,000.
What is the explanation of this?

This is for repairs to the west breakwaters, covering three lengths of 496, 134 and 31 feet, respectively, which were severely damaged by storms. This is a very important port, and the works cannot be allowed to go into disrepair.

I understand
that there is a vote in the Supplementary Estimates also for repairs to Port Col-borne.

My hon. friend no
doubt refers to the vote that is being asked for by the Railway Department for repairs to the elevator at Port Colborne.

Item agreed to.
Rondeau - harbour repairs and improvements, $10,000.
What is that?

This vote is required
to complete the contract let to the Border Cities Construction Company for the reconstruction of 227 feet of superstructure of the west pier; also to complete the contract for the construction of a close-faced sheet-pile wall, 320 feet long, and for general repairs to the decking on both piers.

Item agreed to.	.
Thessalon - tv, complete reconstruction of wharf, $12,250.
You are asking for more than the amount of the contract.

In addition to the
contract price there are certain charges that have to be carried, such as inspection, advertising, and other contingencies that are always connected with a work of this character. The engineers in their estimates always include a percentage for contingencies that may develop during construction.

Is not the inspection
done by the officers of the department?
No. As a rule on works of this kind outside inspectors are engaged.
Somebody in the locality, I suppose?
Yes. All these works come under the direction of the district engineers, who have a general supervision over the work, but somebody has to be there all the time to check materials, and so forth.
Are these inspectors appointed by the Civil Service Commission?
Yes.

Does my hon.
friend mean to say that the district engineer names a local inspector, who then has to be appointed by the Civil Service Commission?
Will the minister explain this item?

This revote is required to remove the old rotted superstructure and reconstruct with concrete the remainder of the wharf, consisting of the outer 115 feet by 20 feet, and the headblock 100 feet by 25 feet.
What constituency is that in?
East Algoma.

Why is that necessary
this year if it was not necessary last year?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Manitoba-harbours and rivers generally_
repairs and improvements, $15,000.

What harbours and
rivers are included in this?

A general vote is taken for each province to take care of the small emergency repairs that may be required during the year. The expenditure in the province of Manitoba under this head last year was $9,030.26.
Where?

It was impossible to get what was regarded as reasonable prices for doing the work the previous year, but last August tenders were called again, and one of $10,770 was received, the others running to $18,000 and even over. The chief engineer's estimate was $11,447, and as the lowest tender was well within that mark it was accepted.

This is the list:
Generally	
He Pas Wharf	 _ _ _
Winnipeg Office Staff	"
Delta Protection Works	
Sale of Twin Screw Steamer at Selkirk, Man	
High Bluff	
Victoria Beach Protection

Total
I understand there was a sum of money spent on this general vote last year upon The Pas wharf.
There was also a vote in the Estimates for this particular item last year of $14,800. Has all of that amount been spent in addition to this other amount?
Yes. The larger sum my hon. friend mentions was spent under contract, but this smaller amount was for necessary repairs and the expenditure was carried out by the department itself.
On the same wharf?
The larger sum was spent in extension of the wharf at The Pas. The amount of $1,294 was spent on repairs to the inner part of the wharf.

Item agreed to.
Selkirk-repairs to wharf, $15,000.
This wharf is in Selkirk town?
Yes.
What has been the total cost up to date in connection with it?
The total expenditure for all purposes on this wharf, including dredging un to March 31, 1920, was $101,095.14.'

Item agreed to.
The Pas Wharf, $7,000.
Where is this wharf?
In the constituency of Nelson.
What was the amount of traffic at this wharf last year?

The District Engineer, Mr. Burbridge, reporting on the commercial necessity of this wharf, states that the extension of the present wharf is required to handle increasing traffic coming to and leaving the port of The Pas. This port is the distributing point for all points on the Saskatchewan river and its tributaries. One firm handled 800 tons of freight alone, and 7,500 tons of copper ore were landed at The Pas . in 1920. The Provincial Government I am informed is building a railway to the large copper deposits of Northern Manitoba, and the material to be used will have to be handled by water.

Item agreed to.

Alice Arm-wharf-conditional on Provincial Government building road, $18,500.
According to the item, this work is conditional on the Provincial Government building a road. What does that mean?

Alice Arm is a mining town of growing importance a hundred miles north of Prince Rupert. The population at present is approximately 400. A regular boat service is maintained by the Union Steamship Company to Vancouver, and considerable quantities of supplies, mining machinery, etc., will go into the country in the next few years. A short rail line from the proposed wharf to the Dolly Varden mines will be built.
Is this a new wharf?

This vote has been
asked for and granted year by year. The construction has been delayed in view of a prospective understanding with the Provincial Government that a road would be built to connect the wharf with the district which will be served by the wharf. The road is under contract now. The Provincial Government have given a contract for its completion and it is anticipated that the construction of the wharf will be proceeded with.

How
much has been spent on the construction to date?
Nothing.
Is it a new Wharf?
Yes.
Is not that a departure from the general policy laid down, that no new works will be undertaken?

It was decided some
years ago to construct this wharf and a vote has appeared in the Estimates from year to year. The Estimate this year is therefore only a revote, the policy in regard to this construction having been decided, presumably, when the vote was first granted. As I have explained, the construction was deferred because of negotiations with the Provincial Government, and it is felt that it would hardly be proper, now that they have fulfilled their part of the bargain and have agreed to build the road, that we should recede from the undertaking.

We are being told in
all other parts of the country that no new wharves will be undertaken, and the

non. minister is not living up to the principle he has laid down. I am afraid he will find this departure embarrassing for him elsewhere.
In what constituency is this work to be done?
Skeena.

Item agreed to.
Boswell-floating: wharf, $8,500.
Is this a new construction?
It is a new construction but it is also a revote.

The hon. member for
Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) is perfectly right. The fact that these things may have been decided upon years ago is no excuse for commencing new constructions now, when we have no money. Expenditures should be curtailed, and I for one protest against any money being voted for new wharves or any other new public works.

This is a float that
takes the place of a pile wharf that was destroyed by storms. In one sense it is a new work, but as it takes the place of a structure which has been serving the business of the district, my hon. friend will admit that it is hardly in the category of new undertakings.

There are works in
the city of Quebec which were stopped when the war broke out. They are still unfinished, and it is not fair for this House to vote money for new construction when works already begun are not being completed.

I endorse the remarks of the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). In Quebec we have been asking for repairs to a wharf destroyed by the flood in 1918, but the Government has always stated that they had no money. If they have no money for Quebec, how is it that they can afford expenditures somewhere else?

If my hon. friend will
refer to the Estimates he will find that there is provision for works in the province of Quebec. The task of keeping up structures is a difficult one; it is not easy to determine exactly when repairs should be gone on with and when works .should be allowed to stand over for another year. The officials of the department are very often put to it to correctly draw the line.
I can assure my hon. friend that every effort is being made to care for the works that are in urgent need of attention throughout the country, and if he will look at the Estimates he will find that his province has not been neglected.
I did not mean the province, I meant the city of Quebec.

Item agreed to.	\
Carroll's Landing-wharf, $11,000.
That is a new wharf also.

Those members of the House who were present last year when the Public Works Estimates were under consideration will recollect that the acting minister stated that the appropriations then voted were to be expended. The item under discussion is a revote, and acting on the policy which was outlined last year tenders were asked for this work-it has been advertised and we have received very reasonable tenders to construct.

I accept the minister's word, but I must call his attention to the fact that there were certain amounts voted in the Estimates last year for works in other parts of the country, and I do not find them in the Estimates this year -urgent works too. I have in my mind's eye at the present time an appropriation that was in the Estimates last year, but, so far as I can see, these Estimates do not contain that item.
Is this a new construction also?
Yes, but it is a revote.

Has
the work been commenced?
Yes, tenders were called for and the contract has been awarded.

Tenders were called
for in the case to which I have reference, but, for some reason or other, the contract was not awarded. The appropriation in question was revoted several times.

Will
the minister say when the tenders were called for?

Tenders for this work were called for more than once. Tenders were first invited in August, 1920, and in the opinion of the chief engineer of the department they were all too high-they were above his estimate. In January of

this year tenders were again called for, and a tender $3,000 lower than the lowest tender on the previous occasion was received.

How
much is it?

I hoped to have been able to discuss these questions of expenditure on wharves and harbours with some idea of the public service that these different works were given to our people, and two months ago I put a question on the Order Paper which was passed as an Order for Return. The schedule which should have been prepared, and which I should have had long ere this, would have given the expenditure for the last five years on capital and on operating account of these different wharves, the amount of upkeep which the Government was obliged to expend year Jby year, and the amount of tonnage which these wharves serve. If I could have had, and the House could have had, the advantage of this information we could have discussed these Estimates with considerably more benefit, I think, to the people, and I deeply regret that the Government was not able to give me this information. It is very hard for us, Mr- Chairman, to really criticise these works as they should be criticised, because we cannot tell just how much public benefit each wharf affords to the people of Canada.

The return which my hon. friend asked for is, as he knows, a voluminous one which necessitates going into the departmental records for the past five years of all public expenditures on harbours and rivers. I am sure he quite underrates the amount of clerical work necessary to produce the figures that he asks for. I will make inquiry of the department and expedite the compilation of the return in every possible way consistent with the carrying on of the other duties with which the officials are charged.

Item agreed to.
Fraser River ('lower)-operation of snag boat, $30,000.
What is that for?

As the name implies
it is a boat for the removal of snags. In navigation, as in other pursuits, snags should always be avoided wherever possible. Snags come down the Fraser river and are a great menace to navigation. The department some years ago went into the removal of these, and all the reports we [Mr. McCurdy. 1
have are to the effect that the expenditure is one which has been more than amply justified.

Who
owns this snag boat?

The Department of
Public Works.

Item agreed to.
Graham-wharf, $7,700.

This also is a new
wharf.

This work is under
contract.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers generally-repairs and improvements, $95,000.
This vote appears in a very general way. Has the minister any information in regard to what he proposes to do under it?

As my hon. friend
knows, the coast line of British Columbia is very extensive, and the people are dependent altogether, in many places, on water transportation. I have a list of the expenditures made last year on these sundry works, and it occupies a page and a half in the Estimate book. I will send the information to my hon. friend if he would like to peruse it.

How much of the
$95,000 was spent last year?
Why is it necessary to expend any more than that amount this year?
It may not be expended. The expenditure may be much smaller this year, but we want to be on the safe side.
The minister expended only $35,000 last year. Why have such a wide margin? Would it not be better to take a smaller vote?

I would like to point this out to the committee. It is largely a question of emergency in these repairs. As the minister explained, the coast line of the province is exceedingly long. You have Queen Charlotte island, Vancouver island, and all the coast line of British Columbia, with innumerable wharves at small places which are completely isolated and dependent wholly on this method of transportation. Now the vote may not be needed, but on

the other 'hand, emergencies may arise. For instance there may be violent storms, like one storm of a year ago in which a whole wharf was washed away.
There may be an election, too.
The vote is the same as last year.

The emergencies are not more likely to happen this year than last year when only $35,000 was expended. For my hon. friend to ask for almost three times the amount that he knows from experience is likely to be required is entirely too much of a margin. I therefore move that the item be reduced by the sum of $45,000.
Amendment negatived on division: Yeas, 35; nays, 44.

I beg to call the attention of the Chairman to the fact that I counted thirteen 'members on the other side, even including my hon. and good friend the Minister of Finance, who came in after the question was put and the vote was being taken. I want to know if, when we are in committee, a member has to hear the question before he can vote on it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The point of order
raised by (the hon. mqmber for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) has often been decided before by the Chairman of Committee, both by the present incumbent and by his predecessors. A vote in committee is not a recorded vote. Any hon. member who is present in the chamber when the vote is being taken has the right to vote for or against the motion, and it is not necessary for him to state whether he heard the question put, or not.

What constitutes the
taking of the vote; is it standing up and hearing the question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The taking of the
vote consists in putting the question and counting the members.

Item agreed to.
loco-wharf, $9,200.

This is to take the
place of a wharf that fell into utter decay and could not be repaired.
Is it new construction?

All construction, under
votes granted by this House is new, but in
the sense I have explained this is not new construction, it takes the place of a wharf that has fallen down.

We cannot hear'the
minister at all.

The minister
states that all construction under these items is new, whether so indicated or not. Now we have an item for loco which is simply marked "wharf," and the minister states that it is a renewal. The next item, Kincolith, is marked "wharf renewal." There it is clearly indicated that it is to replace an old wharf.

I think I can explain
that to the satisfaction of my hon. friend. At loco there was an old structure that became so dilapidated that it was impossible to repair it. Similar facilities are being created at the same place.
Is the new wharf on the same site?

A very short distance
away.

In what constituency
is this loco wharf located?

I can answer that. It
is situated at a small town called loco, of about 3,000 population, twelve miles distant from Vancouver. There are huge oil tanks and refineries located there.

Is it on the seashore,
or on the river?

It is on the upper
reaches of Burrard Inlet.

Item agreed to.
Kuskanook-wharf, $5,800.

Is that new
construction?

If the hon. gentleman
will look at the item he will see that it is a revote.

I am asking a
question of the minister.
It does appear to be a revote, but as the money was not spent last year it would look as if this was proposed for new construction.
The item-

We do not need a
lecture from the hon. member for North
Simcoe (Mr. Currie). The fact that it is a revote does not indicate that it is new construction. He should learn himself, before teaching others.

This proposed work is
in the same class as one dr two other items which we have discussed. This is a revote, but for a new structure. After the authorization by Parliament last year, contracts were entered into and the work is now proceeding.

Item agreed to.	.
Ladysmith-wharf, $12,000.
Is that a revote of last year's general Estimates or was it in the Supplementaries ?

I am informed it was
in the Supplementary Estimates of last year.

Item agreed to.
Manson's Landing-wharf, $6,500.
Is that another new wharf?

This item is for a new
wharf.

In regard to all these wharves that are new construction, and said to be revotes, which I have no doubt they are, what is the reason for the increase in the amount required if no money has been spent? Take the case of Boswell, vote increased from $6,500 to $8,500; Carroll's Landing, vote increased from $7,000 to $11,000; loco, vote increased from $3,000 to $9,200; Ladysmith, vote increased from $9,500 to $12,000. What is the necessity for these increases?

In the case of Manson's Landing the amount asked last year was $5,500. Since that appropriation was made tenders have been called for and it has been found impossible to complete the work for that amount, the sum of $6,500 being necessary. It is not much of an advance; in some cases there are decreases.
The vote for Manson's Landing is indicated as a revote, but I do not find it in the main Estimates of last year.
The records show that this is a revote and that the original vote was made in the Supplementary Estimates of last year.

Item agreed to,

Princess Creek-floating wharf, $2,300.

Are
these floating wharves moved from one place to another? Do they serve more than one locality?
No. It is a less expensive method of providing facilities that the department has adopted largely in British Columbia, where the water level changes.

Are these pontoon
wharves or solid log floats?
Solid logs, I believe.

I cannot quite understand the minister's explanation with regard to these increases. He has pointed out that these items were put in the Estimates last year and that tenders were called, but on account of the tenders being too high the works, were not built. Am I right in that?
In some cases, yes.

This year amounts are
asked for much in excess of last year's votes. My hon. friend either has more money or there has been a change of policy. I would like an explanation of the anomaly.

Take, for instance, the vote asked for under the head of Carroll's Landing, where $11,000 is asked for, the vote last year being $7,000. It was the intention of the department that the work should be proceeded with even if it should cost more than the $7,000 asked for last year. When the Estimates were being made up this year the construction costs were still high and lower tenders had not been received. The deputy minister advises that the present Estimate was based on tenders which had been received. It was a matter for the department to decide whether the project should be laid aside or a vote sufficiently large to complete the work asked for.

I think we are entitled to an explanation from the minister as to the reason for the difference between appropriations for public works in different parts of the country. I know of instances where applications which have come to the Government for public works have been met with the reply that, on account of the state of the country's finances, the policy of the department was to start no new works, and public works which have been started have been suspended for the same reason. But now we find that new works are being started in other parts of the

country. We are entitled to know the reason for this discrimination.

The
minister should be able to give us some explanation in regard to this matter. In Nova Scotia repairs have not been made to existing works. In my county a certain breakwater at Half Island Cove was partly broken down by storm in 1919. It was reported to the department that a very small sum would effect the necessary repairs, but no action was taken. The department was notified that if the matter was allowed to stand for another winter a large sum would be required for repairs, but it was allowed to stand and the breakwater went to pieces; now it will take $10,000 or $12,000 to make repairs that might have been made earlier for a couple of thousand dollars. That is the way repairs have been attended to in my constituency, and it is hard to understand why we should embark on a large number of new works when conditions of that kind prevail-where old works have been allowed to go into the sea because the Government would not provide a small sum to repair damages caused by storms.

I agree that the amount asked for public works is not generous, even if adequate to meet real necessities. My bon. friend, who is <an observant man, sion of alleged public facilities, the commercial necessity of which has been doubtful. Would he say that the small sums which can be spared for public works should be utilized in the keeping up of structures of value to a few people, and that the needs of much larger communities should be ignored? No matter what policy is adopted, there must be exceptions to the rule. We had a discussion this afternoon about loco, B.C., where a large community, about three thousand people, has grown up, where there are huge oil tanks and refineries, and where, if there is no new construction, the community must do without necessary facilities. It is difficult at all times for the officials to tell exactly where to draw the line, they exercise their best discretion in these oases; and the few cases where small hew structures are being undertaken are at places where the commercial necessity has been great. I think the committee will agree that where this committee in a previous year authorized the expenditure of money at certain places, the department should go ahead and provide those facilities. Otherwise, when Parliament met again and the Estimates of
the department were brought down, the department would be subject to the criticism that they had a warrant to go ahead and provide those facilities and that they had failed to do so. While it is difficult to decide where to draw the line, practically no new constructions have been authorized. I am sure I am within the mark if I say that, including the class of representation to which the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) has referred, requests have come to the department this year for the expenditure of over $100,000,000, while the total amount involved in carrying to completion works at present under contract, repairs to old contracts and isolated cases of new construction, is in these Estimates something less than $5,000,000. Not a day passes but one or two or three, sometimes half a dozen, delegations come to the department, and I am sure my hon. friend from Quebec (Mr. Lapointe), if he were administering a department of Government having to do with the expenditure of money on public works, would advise them along the line that I have always advised them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must ask hon.
gentlemen to refrain from conversation. We have reached the point where it is practically impossible for even the Chairman to know what item hon. members are discussing.

As these are contracts to be let, I think it is not in the public interest that the minister should be asked to disclose the estimate of the department. It would simply be giving information to the contractors. It has never been done in the House before, to my knowledge.

The minister is asking for
$500,000 for certain work in the Maritime Provinces, and I think the committee is entitled to be informed as to how this amount is to be divided up between the different provinces.

So far as the work to
be done by departmental dredges is concerned, I do not think the public interest would suffer if I gave the figures, but perhaps my hon. friend would assent to the proposal that in cases where tenders are to be called for close approximation of the cost as arrived at by our engineers should not be made public.
I quite agree.

The following proposed dredging for New Brunswick is on the programme for this year. Grand Anse, 9,000 cubic yards; Hatfield Point, 7,000 cubic yards,-for both of these we expect to ask tenders; Miramichi bay, 75,000 cubic yards, at a cost probably of $22,500; Molus river, Kent, N.B. 7,000 cubic yards; Nelson, 3,750 cubic yards; Newcastle to Bridgetown,
30,000	cubic yards, at a cost probably of $15,000; Restigouche river, 190,000 cubic yards, at a cost probably of $57,000; Bathurst, N.B., 88,000 cubic yards, at a probable cost of $26,400; Douglastown, Northumberland County, 7,500 cubic yards, at a probable cost of $4,500. Dredging will also be done at other places.
In regard to Hatfield Point, is the work to be done on the St. John river or on the main shore?
It is on the river, I understand.
Has any dredging been done there recently?
No.

What shipping does my
hon. friend expect there?
I shall get the information and forward it to my hon. friend.

A year or two ago there was an appropriation of $1,200 for work on the St. Charles river, which was not expended. Both the St. Charles and the St. Louis rivers should be dredged, for

the convenience of farmers who have their fertilizer brought up the river in scows: 1 do hope that an amount for this purpose will be included. I think the farmers in that part of the country have cause for complaint, and I therefore feel it is my duty to bring the need for this work before the minister.

I would like some information in regard to the proposed dredging in the province of Nova Scotia. There are two urgent cases in my own constituency. One is at Port Hilford. For the last ten years this Government has been asked to expend a small amount in dredging the harbour at Port Hilford so as to enable the coasting steamer to reach the wharf in stormy weather. Repeated requests have been made for this work, and we have been informed on several occasions that something would be done, but so far as I know, nothing has been done up to the present time. The sand has filled in around the wharf so much that on a stormy day the coasting steamer is unable to get to the place where the shelter is. The harbour is an exposed one and the steamer is not able to call at all when the weather is rough, owing to the fact that the dredging has not been done. The other case is the harbour of Canso, where some dredging has been done in the last few years to remove the boulders. This is a very important port, the headquarters of the fishing industry in eastern Nova Scotia, and it is urgent that the dredging work there should be completed. I should like to know from the minister whether provision has been made for dredging at these two places out of this vote for $500,000.

I have no recollection of having had the necessity for dredging at Port Hilford drawn to my attention since I assumed charge of the department. There is no amount included in this vote for dredging at Port Hilford, and the same applies to the harbour of Canso. There was a request received from Canso some two months ago for the construction of a new wharf at that place, but no representations! have been made to me with regard to dredging at that port.

What was the reason that my hon. friend did not make any provision for the construction of that wharf? Its construction is of very special importance to the fishermen of the locality. It serves not only as a wharf,
but also as a shelter to a part of the harbour. The request the minister speaks of was made by the Fishermen's Union of Canso, which is a very strong and influential body, and very important from a commercial standpoint. The expenditure would not be very large, and it certainly would be a justifiable expenditure if any exception is to be made to the rule* The minister has already made half a dozen exceptions to the rule in British Columbia, and I therefore shall find it difficult to explain to my constituents why something was not done in connection with the wharf at Canso. What is the reason?

Different representations have been received from Canso with respect to the necessity for this work. I have not had the same opportunity of personally acquainting myself with the conditions there, as my hon. friend has. He says that the wharf is very much needed, but I am informed that in the meantime there are other means of loading and unloading fishing cargoes that come into that port. I have no personal knowledge of that, of course, but the representations are that this work is not of such extreme urgency as if no other wharf existed at the port. There are privately-owned wharves at Canso which for years have been used by the fishermen. The fishermen say that this is not satisfactory, but the fact is that they have been using these wharves for years.

They
are private wharves not generally available to the public.

I have no doubt that if either the hon. member or I wanted to land a cargo there we could. I understand that no charge is made for the use of these wharves. It is true they are privately owned, but they are used by the public. So that while it would be desirable to have a fishermen's wharf there when conditions permit, it was decided that it was not in the class of urgency that it could not stand over for another year.

Will
you build it next year?

Will the
minister give the amount of this vote that will be spent in Prince Edward Island, and also outline the programme for this season, informing us just where the money will be spent?

If it would make no difference. I think the minister might fin-

ish the outline of his programme with regard to Nova Scotia.
My heart is there.
Certainly, and if my hon. friend has no objection the minister might finish Nova Scotia first.

Dredge No. 1, the
" Fielding," is to operate this year at Liverpool and remove 50,000 cubic yards, at an estimated cost of $20,000. She will then proceed to Restigouche river to remove 190,000 cubic yards at a cost of $57,000.
Restigouche is not in Nova Scotia.

Well, she gets a good start in Nova Scotia. My hon. friend from Queen's (Mr. Sinclair) has asked a question in regard to Prince Edward Island. Perhaps I had better take the programme province by province. I will answer the hon. member for Queen's first. The programme for dredging operations in Prince Edward Island is not definitely concluded yet, but work is to be begun by the dredge at the marine wharf at Charlottetown, to remove 18,000 odd cubic yards of material. After that it will proceed to Pownal wharf and then probably to Murray River.	,
What portion of this $500,000 is to be spent in Prince Edward Island?
The minister says that the programme for the season is not yet fully made up. How long is it estimated that the dredge will be required to carry out the work he has outlined?
Pretty nearly the whole season.

In 1914, or perhaps somewhat earlier-I am not sure of the exact date but it was before the war, at any rate-the Department of Public Works began the work of straightening and making a proper channel in the Hillsborough river from Charlottetown to Mount Stewart. The work was only partially completed when the war broke out, when it was thought wise to defer it owing to other heavy expenditures. If the work that is contemplated during the coming summer is completed before the close of the season, and the dredge is likely to be idle, I would suggest that the minister consider continuing the work of improving the

channel in the Hillsborough river.
I am sure the dredge mentioned will not be idle, however, I will make a memorandum of what my hon. friend says and see whether the dredge can be placed on the work he has mentioned.
I think the minister says that there is something like $45,000 to be spent on the Restigouche river. Is that right?
Is the bulk of this work being done by Government dredges?
Yes, almost entirely.

Well, I can appreciate the difficulty of specifying definite sums at particular points, because the dredges have to be maintained anyhow, and they start at one point and go to another. In that way several provinces become mixed up. I fancy that these estimates which the minister gives are made up in this way: From the general work of the department they know what it will cost to remove certain classes of material, and applying that rough estimate to the quantity they have to remove they are able to give an approximate idea of what it will cost. But it is difficult to give an appropriation of a particular sum to a particular place. Am I right in assuming that the bulk of the work is to be done by Government dredges?

Yes, that is perfectly so, and the method by which I have arrived at the estimated expenditure is exactly as my hon. friend has indicated. That is why I think it would be just as useful if I were to indicate the cubic yards which the department hopes to remove.

If the minister has an estimate of the amounts he will spend in various harbours, that is all we ask for. I presume he will not go at the work in a haphazard manner, commencing at one end of a province without knowing where he will go next. The order in which the work is to be done is not a matter of interest to the committee at present; all we ask for is information as to where the various sums will be spent. My hon. friend has not yet told us very much about Nova Scotia.

No, for the very good reason that I have been interrupted several times when trying to do so. If I am allowed to proceed I will give the information. First, at Glace bay, 22,000 yards; at Liverpool, 50,000 yards; at Port Hood,

3,750 yards; at Shenacadie, 27,600 yards; at St. Peter's Narrows, 17,000 yards; at Sydney, 36,000 yards; at Windsor, 2,000 yards; at Yarmouth, 110,000 yards.
Am I right in supposing that Restigouche river was one of the places mentioned by the minister where dredging operations will take place?

We expect to dredge
190,000	cubic yards in the Restigouche river this year.
What will be the approximate cost?
Probably $60,000.
At what point will this work be done?
At the Grandoon flats.

Is there
anything for Cross Point?

There is a small amount under another heading that is going to be spent at Cross Point. I might also say that one of the dredges is now on her way to New Carlisle where 12,000 cubic yards are to be excavated.
As a matter of fact are all the Government dredges employed all the time?
Oh, no. Several Government dredges are laid up; they have not been in operation and will not be in operation this year.
I will bear what my hon. friend has said in mind.

Item agreed to.
Dredging-Ontario and Quebec, $450,000.
May I ask the minister if this vote includes any expenditure for dredging in Yamaska county?
There are no Public Works dredges operating in Yamaska at the present time.
I have seen some of them at work.

Would
the minister be kind enough to mention the places where dredging is being done in the province of Quebec?

At Batiscan, 32,500
cubic yards; Doucet's Landing, 22,000 cubic yards; at Harricanaw, in the county of Pontiac, 24,000 cubic yards; Rimouski,
80,000	cubic yards; River du Loup, 80,500 cubic yards; and Verdun and Laprairie, removal of boulders necessitating the expenditure probably of $1,000. This is in addition to the dredging at New Carlisle, of which I have already spoken.
Item agreed to.
Roads and Bridges-Banff-bridges, $168,000.

Under the general vote for roads and bridges I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the condition of a bridge in the county of Pontiac, crossing the Ottawa river, which has been in charge of the Department of Public Works for some years. A few years ago they replaced two of the piers, but the centre pier is now in need of repair. I understand that the minister had a deputation wait upon him from the village of Bryson to ask that the work be gone on with as the bridge had been condemned by the minister's own department. It is the only means of communication between the village of Bryson, on the mainland, and Calumet island, which is an important farming district. Because the deputation did not ask my hon. friend to construct a bridge on the other side of the island to connect with the province of Ontario, he saw fit to refuse to maintain his bridge at that point. He was quick enough, however, when he found an item for dredging in the county of Pontiac to say that it was for work in my constituency. Perhaps the fact that this bridge is in the constituency of Pontiac was his reason for refusing to maintain the structure in a condition in which it can be used. The bridge cost a great deal of money and is liable, I understand, to collapse at any time-it is not safe for traffic. Although there is a steel superstructure the Government apparently are not maintaining this bridge in good repair. I think the minister should bring in an item in the Supplementary Estimates to take care of the repairs to this bridge. It is not fair to say to the township in which the bridge is located that they should have to look after it; the minister should provide, in the Supplementary Estimates, for doing this necessary work.

It is not intended, Mr. Chairman, to provide any sum for the repairs of this bridge. I recall quite distinctly the conversation that took place when the delegation came to see me some months ago in connection with this matter The delegation was headed by Mr. Rimer, mayor of Bryson, and two other gentlemen, who asked that the department continue to repair a bridge of a local character connecting an island with another place on the mainland in the county of Pontiac. If, as my hon. friend has suggested, the bridge went from the island across the Ottawa river it would be interprovincial in its character, and under the British

North America Act probably a case could be made out for the department contributing to its maintenance. I referred the matter to the Department of Justice. The answer being that it was not a work which the Dominion Government could be called on to maintain, I think I would be less than frank if I allowed my hon. friend to believe that any sum will be forthcoming towards its upkeep. The delegation which visited Ottawa have been advised of the decision of the department, which, so far as I know, can be looked upon as final.

As my hon. friend knows, the Ottawa river is the boundary line between the provinces of Quebec and Ontario clear to the north end of Lake Timiskam-ing, and the only bridges that cross the river between the St. Lawrence and that point are built from the Quebec side to the Ontario side and land on an island in every case. The bridge at Ottawa here was built and is maintained by the Government. The same remark applies to the bridge at Portage du Fort. The municipality and the province built this originally, and the Dominion Government recognized the injustice of asking them to maintain it, as it was on interprovincial waters. But now that the minister finds a loop-hole to escape this liabality he avails himself of it. I think the course taken is entirely unfair, especially when we have items here of hundreds of thousands of dollars for bridges in other parts of the country, some of them new structures. If the Government are maintaining bridges across interprovincial waters, there is absolutely no excuse why they should not maintain this bridge. The only difference in this case is that my hon. friend has got a bridge only half way across the river, and because he has not built the other half he refuses to maintain the part that is built.

If the districts affected will bring forward a proposal to make this an interprovincial bridge by extending it across the Ottawa river, I shall be very glad to have the matter taken into consideration; but at present it is simply a local bridge built by the local authorities.
How often has the minister consulted the Department of Justice in relation to public works in constituencies represented by his friends on the other side of the House?
Whenever there is any necessity.

The minister has had several deputations from

Campbellton asking for an interprovincial bridge between Crosspoint and Campbellton. How does that matter stand?
It stands, Mr. Chairman.

An interprovincial bridge was built some years ago at Matapedia by this Government in conjunction with the Governments of Quebec and New Brunswick. I have called attention to the approaches of this bridge, as the road running through unorganized territory is almost impassable, and it is the only leading thoroughfare between Quebec and New Brunswick. The former member for Rimouski had some $10,000 expended on the road, but for some years no further work has been done. I wish the minister would give the matter attention and see if something cannot be done.

I have received similar requests from the people of Campbellton and vicinity. I called upon the minister at the beginning of the session, but he told me the treasury was rather short of money, and that the structure being purely an interprovincial bridge, no federal assistance could be given. But interprovincial bridges have been built by the Dominion Government, and I can cite a case in point 

the bridge between Ottawa and Hull. The necessity of a bridge between Campbellton and Crosspoint is just as great, and the bridge between here and Hull is certainly a precedent in favour of federal assistance in this instance.

I want to make a suggestion to the minister in regard to the Grand Etang bridge in Inverness county. The Government is spending considerable money on repairs to this bridge every second or third year, and when any further repairs are contemplated I would ask the minister to take into consideration its removal up to the Narrows. This would accomplish two purposes: it would give a shorter and less expensive bridge, and would also furnish the fishermen with urgently needed accommodation for the protection of their boats, as at present the harbour is entirely too small. This is an urgent matter and I would respectfully suggest that the minister take it into consideration when any further expenditure is needed for repairs to the existing bridge.

I shall see that the hon. member's suggestion is borne in mind.

Is it the intention of the minister to undertake this expenditure this year?

Yes. It is partly for
diversion, in order to get a more direct line.
Graving docks, locks and dams, etc., $150,200.

How
many graving docks does the Government own?

The three mentioned
in this vote and one at Kingston.
Is the new graving dock that is being built at Esquimalt the property of the Government?
Yes.

I understood that the Government paid subsidies to private companies to build these docks. If I remember rightly, my hon. friend's predecessor told us that a move was on foot for the construction of a graving dock at Vancouver by a company, subsidized by the Government. How is it that the graving dock at Esquimalt is on a different basis from the docks at Colling-wood, Vancouver and other points?

There are two systems under which docks have been built in Canada. There is the Dry Dock Subsidies Act, the provisions of which are availed of by people who wish to build docks, the locations, of course, to be approved by the Government. Under that Act docks have been built at Collingwood, Port Arthur, Montreal and Prince Rupert and subsidy agreements are outstanding for the construction of dry docks at Vancouver and St. John. In addition, the Government have constructed the three which I have mentioned and are constructing the dry dock at Esquimalt, which will serve also the purposes of a naval dock.

Has
the policy of the Government changed in this matter? Is it now to be the policy of the Government to 'build and maintain graving docks and to abandon the old system of insisting that a company manage them and pay the interest on their loans? May other parts of Canada apply to the minister to obtain graving docks similar to the dock now being built at Esquimalt and on the same terms?

As for requests that may come from other parts of the country for additonal dry docks, I would prefer to decide the matter when the applications arrive. I must confess that I am not thoroughly familiar with every detail of what has transpired regarding dry docks that have been under construction except so far as the records go, but in general I would say that there has been no change in policy.

Item agreed to.

I wish to ask the minister for some information in reference to the extension of the line from Point Sapin to Kouchibouguac in the county of Kent.
I see no vote for that purpose.
Will there be a vote for it in the Supplementary Estimates?
Quite probably so.
What has been the revenue from these different telegraph and telephone lines for the past year?

I have not that information under my hand, but it was given in the annual report of the Department of Public Works which was tabled at the beginning of the session; I will secure a copy and forward it to my hon. friend. But the operation of the Government telegraph and telephone lines covered by this vote is not a commercial undertaking. It is a large annual expense to operate these lines; I suppose the deficit would rujn frotm $600,000 to $700,000 per annum. As a rule these lines serve districts where commercial companies could not profitably operate. For instance, there are lines in certain parts of northern British Columbia and extending to the Yukon, where service is maintained at & heavy annual loss. It is, however, a service which cannot very well be abandoned; I am sure that hon. members would not like to see the Yukon deprived of telegraphic communication. In Eastern Canada these lines are for the most part in sparsely settled districts where there would be no service if it was not provided by the Government.

In connection with the Yukon system, there is considerable duplication; for some distance you will find in little towns along the Grand Trunk Pacific two telegraph offices, those of the Grand Trunk Pacific and those of the Yukon telegraph system. It is some

distance east of Hazelton where the Yukon telegraph line strikes off from the Grand Trunk Pacific and crosses over! to the Canadian Pacific at Ashcroft. I fail to see why it is necessary to maintain two telegraph and telephone offices in each of these towns along that part of the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific which is paralleled by the Yukon system. It seems to me that a saving could be effected in that regard; where the Yukon system strikes the Grand Trunk Pacific telegraphic line you could cut the system and not duplicate from there on to the point where it leaves the Grand Trunk Pacific and goes across to Ashcroft on the Canadian Pacific line.
The line serves a number of places between Hazelton and Ashcroft.

I am asking
the minister, not the hon. member.

I have been giving some attention to this matter, and I quite agree with what my hon. friend states, namely, that there is ground for making improvements by which the services necessary may retained and a considerable saving effected. That is a matter which will receive attention at an early date.
How many miles of telegraph lines are there in New Brunswick?

I have not the information for the province of New Brunswick. It is contained in the annual report which was tabled at the beginning of the session. Altogether the department operates 11,821 miles of land lines, 336 miles of submarine cables, and it has 1,179 offices.

What lines
do the Government operate in Saskatchewan?-because in that province we are very well served. We have a government long-distance system, and the rural systems belong to the farmers, private companies.
I assumed that, this matter being all outlined in the report, hon. members would have it. I regret that at the moment I have not the exact information under my hand.
Is the information in the annual report?
Yes.
Then I will look it up.

Rentals	 469,776
Maintenance of existing buildings.. ..	173,965

130,000	for rents, what buildings are rented in Ottawa and what is the policy of the Government in regard to this matter? Harbours and rivers-Nova Scotia, $274,050. Mr. SINCLAIR (Guysborough) : Will the minister explain the second item, Bass river wharf? Is that a new wharf?
It is for replacement of a wharf that has gone down.

What
is the business at that point?

This is a revote. The principal industries are lumbering and the manufacture of furniture. Located at Bass river is the Dominion Chair Company whose imports of general merchandise approximate $75,000 to $80,000 annually, and whose exports of chairs ordinarily amount to $20,000 annually, making a total of $100,000. Other local merchants who receive at this port will add $20,000 to $25,000. Shipments of lumber average around 4,000,000 feet annually. The old wharf was built in 1894-95. It was extended in 1901-02 and in 1911-12. The work is under contract. Tenders were called for and the work is under way.
Has the work been commenced?
Yes.

The
output of the fishing industry at Canso is at least ten times the figure that the minister gave.
A million dollars a year?
More than that.
I am glad to hear it.
There is a large population depending upon the wharf that was supposed to be built at Canso and that could be built for a much less sum than the wharf at Bass river.
There is no other wharf at Bass river.

There are a few names in this item which occur in different coun-

ties. Maitland, I presume, is in Hants county. Summerville is to be found at several places.
It is in Hants county.
I am sorry; I thought it was in Queen's.
Blanche is in Shelburne county. We shall provide for Blanche in the Supplementary Estimates.

I quite understand
the difficulty my hon. friend has in making new appropriations, but I hope the Government will be able to make a strenuous effort to provide for necessary repairs. There are throughout the country many works of a useful character which are falling rapidly into decay. I know of several in my constituency. This is a matter in which the Government would have to be advised by the engineers of course; but where they have information from their engineers as to the condition of the works, I hope a strenuous effort will be made to provide the necessary repairs, for two purposes; first in order to accommodate the public, and secondly, to prevent works going into decay. After a few years on our Atlantic coast a work that is neglected goes to pieces very rapidly. All I desire to say further is that I hope in the Supplementary Estimates the minister will be able to make provision for works which his engineers report as useful and urgent.

When may we expect

Mr. MeCURDY:	I think it can be said
that so far as the construction of the lower part of the building is concerned-that is, this floor-it will be absolutely completed this year. I am not referring now to the decorations and some fixings of that kind, but to the main construction work; the

construction in the main hall, and the balance of the work on this floor should be finished this summer. The construction of the tower will probably go on for at least another year after the present year. There is some slight difference of opinion as between the architect and the builders as to the carrying capacity of the tower. That is, the architect thinks it is better to build more slowly and take at least another year, after this year, in constructing the main tower, whereas the contractors would willingly go ahead and finish the work this year as that is (physically possible. In order to be safe, the Parliament Buildings Committee is authorizing the taking of two years at least to construct the tower instead of finishing this summer, as they regard that as the safest plan to follow. Is the
design of the tower finally settled?

Not finally settled. It
is settled a little bit beyond the stage where construction has gone, but a final decision as to the upper part has not yet been reached. It is under consideration, however, and will be decided very soon. I have noticed men
working at night on the tower several times this year which would indicate that there was a desire to rush the work. I am not complaining of the fact, but what is the explanation for taking that course? It must involve extra cost.

The very thing the hon. gentleman speaks of occurred to me and I made inquiries with regard to the work that is going on. I find that the men are required to work in alternate Shifts. They first put up a course of stone and that has to be backed up by a course of concrete. It is impossible to have both gangs working at the same time, so by arrangement one works in the day time and the other follows on and works after
ordinary day hours. There is no overtime being paid in connection with the work.

That would be ai
right if you wished to rush the work, but the hon. gentleman has stated it is not intended to rush it. Will he tell us what amount has been expended up to the present time?
Under what system is this work being done, on a percentage basis or by contract?
By double shifts.
I know, but on what basis is it being done?
Of itself it must make an increase in the cost.

Surely.

The arrangement by
which the men are working in double shifts is not costing any more than if these men worked on alternate days.
Then the night work is not costing any more than the day work?
No.
What has been the total cost up to the present time of the whole thing-building, furniture and everything?
In round numbers the expenditure up to the present time has been $9,000,000.
Does the hon. gentleman remember what the original Estimate was? Of course I know it was much below that.

The original estimate was not for the building we have now. There would have been an overrun of expenditure of probably $1,900,000. As every one knows, the cost of labour and material has advanced from 100 to 140 per cent over the figures that

were current when the contract was made, and necessarily that advance has carried with it an increase in the total cost of the building. But it should always be remembered that we are now having a different structure entirely from what we started out to build, and the extra storey and other additions will cost probably from $2,500,000 to $3,000,000.

The total ultimate
cost is expected to be something over

Did I understand the
minister to say that when the building is completed the total cost will not exceed $10,000,000 including furnishings and fittings?	,
I said the cost would probably be somewhat in excess of $10,000,000. '

made for a chamber to receive a carillon, should it later on be decided to install one. under the direction of the contractors, Peter Lyall & Sons, Limited, and by tender and contract, and the tenders are submitted to the Parliamentary Building Committee for approval before the contracts are awarded.
Does this Parliamentary Building Committee meet?

Yes, it has met on an average perhaps three times a month since I became Minister of Public Works. quantity of Ohio stone which was used for trimmings about the doors and windows because it was employed in the old build-

ing, the stone used is Canadian stone, obtained partly from Wallace, Nova Scotia, and partly from the Tyndall quarries in Manitoba.

What is the inscription on the tower? I cannot make it out.

If I understand the minister correctly, there is a difference of opinion between the architect and the builders in regard to the construction of the tower farther up. Has the architect consulted the architects of other towers? Because this is a serious matter. We are running this tower up 300 feet, and I think a great deal of care should be exercised before the construction is gone on with if there is any difference of opinion between the architect and the builders.

I am afraid I did not make my meaning very clear. What I intended to convey was that while both the builders and the architects are perfectly confident about the enduring qualities of the tower when erected, there was some slight difference of opinion as to whether it would be better to rush the work to completion now or to build 100 or 125 additional feet this summer and allow that to set before going on with the balance in the succeeding year. The committee threw its decision on the side of safety and decided that construction should not proceed very far this year, and that what is built in the next three months shall have time to set before the tower is completed.
I am obliged to the minister for his explanation, because his former answer left me under the impression that the architect and1 the builders were not agreed.
Not at all.
I could not hear distinctly, but I think my hon. friend from Middlesex (Mr. Ross) asked what letters were being inscribed on the tower. *I did not. catch the minister's answer.
Yes, he asked that question and I told him I could not give him the information.
Is there any means of finding that out? Because if the inscription should not be placed there this is a good time to stop it.
Yes, I hope before the committee rises to be able to give my hon. *friend the information.
Has all the compensation to the architect under the original contract been paid?

No, the payments
which are due to the architect have not all been paid. The architect's commissions were to be paid on a fixed sum of $5,000,000, but alterations in the plans took place; a larger and more expensive building has been provided, and on the extra cost the architects are being paid their regular commission.
Two per cent?

No, 51 per cent on
these so-called extras, such as the central heating station and the additional features that have gone into the building.

I do not wish to be understood as expressing any opinion as to what the compensation of these gentlemen should be. They have given us a magnificent piece of work, and I should like to see Mr. Pearson well treated. But my recollection is that when the explanations were last given we were shown that the terms of the contract were such that the architects, under the terms of their contract, got all their money when only half the work was done.

Under their contract they would be entitled to receive all their commission when only $5,000,000 had been expended on the buildings, and doubtless these payments were made. Since that time they have been drawing their fees as against this additional construction.
Then it is admitted that they are to receive extra compensation?
Oh, yes.
I do not think we were informed of that before. I am not complaining at all; I do not want to he ungenerous. My complaint was that the wording of the contract, I thought, was very clumsy.

I think that the feeling expressed by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's will be shared by the members of the House generally. I am sure that the Building Committee are unanimous on the question. They feel that we have a very fine building which reflects credit on the architects and builders and is a fitting home for the Houses of Parliament. I am sure that every hon. member would be sorry if those who were producing this building did so at a financial loss to themselves-the labourer is worthy of his hire. There was an exchange of letters at the time the contract was originally given with reference to limiting the commission to payment on the basis of a cost of $5,000,000. But the contract was not completed and the feeling was unanimous in the committee that further compensation should be given. I trust that that course will meet with general approval; to my mind it is eminently fair and reasonable.

Does my hon. friend think that an architect who is drawing $50,000 a year is suffering very much if he does not get any more than was originally agreed to? I think there should be some definite understanding about what this building is to cost, "when it is to he completed, and what amount by way of extras is to be paid to the contractor and to the architect. I am not at all in favour of this idea that these people are to he pampered and that we should spend money in this extravagant way, allowing them 51 per cent commission on extras because they did not come within a fifty-per-cent guess of what the building would cost. I think that the people of the country would rather condemn the architect who made such a bad guess about his work than agree to pay him 51 per cent on extras. My hon. friend talks about "magnificent work," and so on, but I have not met any person in this chamber who has said that the chamber itself is a very good one. I have not met any person who has been quite satisfied with it. As for the rest of the building-well, the lobbies on the sides here are such that an ordinary Galician farmer in Western Canada would not house his cattle in them.

If my hon. friend's
statement of fact were correct, I would agree with him. But it is not true that the architect is drawing personal fees of $50,000 a year. The operations of the architect require the employment of a large staff and the carrying on of an extensive work in the way of designing, drafting of plans, and oversight of construction. It is not a case of one man drawing these architects' fees; he is paid for his organization in keeping up the work. I know that at times the architect's staff has included eight or ten or more highly-paid assistants-so I am advised by the architect himself; and these services cannot be secured without substantial cost. I think in justice to the architects of the building I should make this matter clear to the committee-that these fees include all the drafting and office staff and all exipenses entailed in the carrying on of the architect's work. If only a commission on the original $5,000,000 were paid I doubt whether the architect would get back a new dollar for an old; I do not think he would have anything for his own services at all. I do not think any member of the committee would like to see an outcome of that kind. Large business firms engaging the services of architects pay them a certain percentage for their professional work, and often the rate is more than 51 per cent. I am informed that the architects' fees in connection with the Sun Life Building in Montreal were between 6 and 7 per cent. The percentage paid in the case of the Parliament Buildings is regarded by those who are in the business as not excessive-indeed, it is looked upon as a modest fee. That being the case, is it not a matter of equity that the architect should receive that fee on whatever the cost of the building is? The cost of the building is not decided by the architect himself; it is a matter for the Building Committee. I repeat that this is a pleasing building, it is one that we can be proud of, and that is the view which has been expressed to me by many hon. gentlemen. Hundreds of people who have visited the building have expressed themselves in similar terms. You cannot have a building of this character without paying for it, and I am sure that members of Parliament will be the last to suggest that we be niggardly in the payment of those who have been responsible for planning and designing the magnificent building.

We were having some information with regard to the building of the tower a few minutes ago, and

I WPS endeavouring to ask a question. I would not undertake to criticise those who are responsible for the erection of this building; I would imagine they were highly trained and competent men. In view of past experience in building towers and public buildings in this city, one naturally views with a good deal of interest the building of a tower such as is now under construction. When the minister intimated that it was going to reach a height of somewhere in the neighbourhood of 300 feet, one can rest assured that there is going to be a tremendous weight resting upon the foundation of the tower. For several years back I have noticed that the outer foundations of the tower are built of concrete; in fact, I think that is the only part of the foundation of the building which is built of concrete. To the ordinary layman, it would appear that the concrete is not of a very good quality. I may be wrong in my estimation of it; but I have noticed that it has checked and that, on two different occasions, it has been gone over with cement and the checks filled in, in order to keep the wet and frost from working on it. This may be purely superficial; I am not saying that there is any serious defect in it; but to the ordinary layman it would appear to be rather an inferior quality of cement. In view of the fact that a tower which was put up in connection with the museum a few years ago, had to be torn down, and that another tower on the West Block tumbled over after it was put up, I am merely throwing out a hint that it might be well to have that matter thoroughly investigated.

I have had no intimation of there being any doubt whatever about the soundness of the structure, and I am quite sure that the apprehensions of my hon. friend are ill founded. . I have pleasure in giving him that assurance, and I am sure he will be pleased to have it. I have discussed this matter quite recently with the contractons, and they are confident that the foundation will bear the weight of the tower. So confident are they, that, as I say, they wish to go ahead and finish the construction this summer, without allowing the nerw work much time to set.

What I said was simply this, that the architect gave an estimate of the cost of reconstruction of the old building. As my hon. friend probably knows, when the old walls were being removed, it was found that it would not do to put a new structure on them; that they were ill-constructed. Alterations had to be made as a consequence of that, and other alterations were made including the addition of a complete storey to the building, with the result that the cost is much larger because you have a much larger building. When
the plan was changed, did the architect
not make a new estimate of what the building he proposed to build would cost?

made.

The drafts on the
treasury.

Have
these inscriptions been put on the tower?
