I do not raise any question, but it will be raised sbmetime or 'another, regarding an inscription in French.

This is a matter that has not come before the Parliamentary Buildings Committee. . I knew, half an hour ago, just as much about it as other members of the House. I have made inquiries since, and the intimation which I have is the result of my inquiries. I solicited an expression of opinion from the House and I am getting it now.
The two languages being official, the point will certainly be raised at some time or other, vand it might as well be considered now.

While I have no objection to the words myself, I can quite understand the point will be raised, and for that reason the hon. gentleman will be well ^advised not to put any such words on at all. I am not objecting to them; but they

would be objected to in other quarters, and we have questions enough of that kind without adding another one.

I should like that attention be drawn to the acoustics of this chamber. It was a great disappointment to myself that the acoustics are not better. This matter has been discussed for a number of years, and every time that the Estimates for the construction of the Parliament buildings has come before this House, the question has been drawn to the attention of the Government. We were assured that we had the best architects that could be found anywhere in Canada attending to this matter, but no one will say that the hearing properties of this chamber are good. There is something the matter with them, and that is one of the greatest difficulties, as regards the chamber. The chamber is very beautiful and comfortable in many ways with the exception of those draughts; but we want to hear one another. That is essential, and in this chamber one cannot hear as well as one should hear. I have a notion that one reason for the trouble is the way in which the ceiling is arranged and the space that exists between the walls and the ceiling. I am not sure whether that makes a difference or not; but I should like the minister to take an interest in this question and, before these architects are paid for the work they have done, they should be compelled to give us a chamber in which we can hear one another. This matter of acoustics must be a scientific question that a skilled architect ought to be able to work out. There are buildings elsewhere in the world that are perfect in that respect, and if there is any building or chamber that we ought to have perfect in that resnect, if possible, it is the House of Commons. This is where the battle of freedom is to be fought in the years to come, and it cannot be intelligently fought unless the representatives of the people can hear one another when they speak. This is a very important matter, and if anything further can be done to make this chamber a place where you can hear men sppak, I trust my hon. friend will give the matter his attention, and endeavour to have the acoustics improved during the recess. I do not think it can yet be too late to take steps to remedy the present condition.

I am sure my hon. friend has noticed an improvement in the acoustic properties of the chamber over

the previous session of Parliament. I have noticed a very distinct improvement myself. Experiments have taken place, the closing of an entrance at one end, for instance, and alterations of a minor character with the idea of improving the acoustics of the chamber. It is, as my bon. friend has said, a scientific question, but he .also know's that acoustics is not an exact science. You cannot get the result that you propose in any given case. I can assure him, however, that the attention of the architects will he drawn to this matter during the recess.

Is not this largely a question for ourselves to tackle? There are certain gentlemen whose voices are clearly heard throughout the chamber. When the Right Hon. Mr. Lowther, the Speaker of the British House, addressed us the other day his voice could be heard in every part of the chamber. My hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) speaks in a low voice, yet his voice penetrates everywhere. You can always hear the voice of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). The trouble with some of us is that we mumble our words and talk in such low tones that I defy any one within three or four feet to hear what is being said. I think it is time for some of us, instead of criticising the architects, to begin and criticise ourselves.

I understand that a little under $9,000,000 has been expended on this building, and I heard the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) say that that was a very lavish expenditure. Personally, I think we have got very good value indeed in this building, as building goes nowadays. I visited the province of Manitoba only a few months ago and went through their building, which is to accommodate only a comparatively few members compared with ours, being a building for one province only with a comparatively small population, yet that building has cost almost as much as this.
That building is used not simply for chamber purposes; it is largely an office building.

I went all through it and I saw the nature of it. It is nothing like the extent of this building/ I repeat, we have got very good value in this building. I think the money has been well expended. When we consider that this building is to stand for at least a hundred 2531
years, perhaps two hundred-it is built of the most durable material and should last a great many more years than that-I cannot agree with the hon. member for Brome that there has been a lavish expenditure, and if the building can be completed for $10,000,000, the cost cannot be called excessive at the present time.
With regard to acoustics, I believe that the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) has given us one of the main reasons why gentlemen are not heard in this chamber. They do not exert themselves when they speak. I have never heard any one complain that he could not hear the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), and there are others who can always be heard-sometimes we hear more than we wish to. It is largely a matter of exerting the voice and trying to make people hear.
I would like to draw the minister's attention to the acoustics of another room, much smaller than this chamber, and that is the Railway Committee room. It is almost impossible to hear a speaker there. You can hear the voice, but the words all seem to run together, and the result is that a great many sentences are lost entirely. It is not because the room is too large, not because the speakers are not speaking up well, but there is something wrong in that room which certainly needs attention.
As to the tower, I hotpe that the very greatest care will be taken in its erection. I have seen one tower fall-in the western block, a few years ago. I happened to be looking out of my window in the direction of the tower, and saw it fall. And another tower was torn down, at the museum. I think we had far better build a tower that is safe than try to reach up too much towards the sky.
"Safety first."

Towers are a great mark for lightning, and we would not like to see a thunderbolt strike the tower of the Dominion House of Commons; that would be a calamity. I have no doubt that the minister has warned all those concerned that the first requisite is safety, and I hope that that is the policy that will be pursued in building the tower. So far as the committee is concerned, I think those that have had to do with it have given us excellent value. I do not know what my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) is accustomed to over the river, when he says that part of this building might be used for housing cattle. This

building appears to me to be on very generous proportions, and all the appliances are of the best, and quite as good, I think, as hon. members are accustomed to in their own home town, if not a little better. Therefore, I think, we ought to be well satisfied, and I hope that the building will be completed in as good a fashion as the work has been done up to date.

Many hon. members have complained of the acoustics of this chamber. There is another room in this building in which the acoustics are too good, and the floor too sonorous altogether, and that is the library. I have never been able to understand, in the twenty years I have been in Parliament, why the floor of the library should not be covered with rubber or matting of some kind. It is almost impossible for a member to work in one of the alcoves of the library because of the noise of people who are walking through. This defect could be remedied in twenty hours or less. It is the only library I know of where the noise is so disturbing to frequenters. If this matter comes under the minister's jurisdiction, I hope he will appropriate the necessary sum of money to remedy this defect. Hon. members and senators on the first and second floors can hear the noise when the employees of the library are walking around to get books from the shelves or replace books that have been returned. This is an important matter, and I hope that the minister will give it his attention.

The question raised by my hon. friend has not, of course, come before the committee, because the floor of the library is just as it was in the olden days. I have no doubt that the reason it has continued so has been because those in charge of the library hesitated to cover up the very fine inlaid floor.
It is no longer pretty.

Well, in some eyes it*
is. Possibly there may have been poor judgment on the part of those in charge, but I have noticed on many occasions the drawback to which the hon. member refers. The library is not directly under the Parliamentary Buildings ^Committee, nor under my direction; it is a joint concern of the Speakers of the Commons and Senate. I shall have the matter brought to their attention, and if I can personally facilitate the rectifying of the evil mentioned I shall certainly see that this is done before Parliament reassembles.

I notice in the Auditor
General's Report, volume 3, page V-18, the commission to Peter Lyall & Sons is 4.4 per cent amounting to $105,613; and the paylists paid by the department amount to $65,600. What does that mean?

That would be the
contractor's paylist paid through the Department of Public Works out of a vote similar (to this made previously.

That is not the question.
If the minister will look at the report he will find that there is mentioned (architect's commission of 4.4 per cent on P. Lyall's bill, $105,000 odd, and paylists paid by the department, of $65,000. There is a commission on that amount also. What is the explanation of that?

While the minister is
looking up this information I might say a word in regard to the acoustics of this Chamber. I went into the Railway Committee room a couple of days ago with Mr. Pearson, the architect, and we tested the acoustics there. We both spoke in raised voices, and he said that the reason why the hearing was so bad there was that the room was not yet fully furnished. The room must have a mat be said, and he added that there was no doubt at all that hearing would improve when the room was properly furnished. He also thinks that this chamber possesses as good acoustic properties as any he has ever known, and he quotes Mr. Lowther, the Speaker of the British House, who spoke here the other day, as saying that in his opinion he had never spoken in a building or in a room which had better acoustic properties than this chamber. The hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) who raised this question almost disproved his own point, for every word he said was perfectly audible over here as far off as I am. The point I wish to make is this: hon. gentlemen have not apparently the mental attitude, when speaking, that is necessary if they wish to be heard. They get up, and instead of speaking, converse across the floor with somebody else and only a few members can hear them. If hon. gentlemen, every time they got .up, would make a speech instead of indulging in what is nothing but a private conversation, there would be no difficulty about hearing them and there Would be no complaint about the chamber. I think that this is a splendidly proportioned chamber, possessing first-rate acoustic properties, and if hon. gentlemen would always observe the rule

which has been laid down by the architect, never to address any one in particular but to look at the clock and speak at the clock, they would make themselves heard and there would be no trouble about the hearing in the chamber.

I can answer the question asked by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill). In the Auditor General's Report there is an item which reads:
Architect's commission of 4.4 per cent on P. Lyall's hill of February, 1919, $105,613.10, pay lists paid by department $65,660.15. Lyall's commission on bill and pay lists, $13,701.86, and voucher of R. W. Hunt & Company, $21.67 ; $8,139.85; paid as follows:	J. A. Pearson,

-or 4.4 per cent commission on these disbursements made on account of the building. I do not know what my hon. friend's question is, but if he wants to know whether Mr. Pearson's commission is on the total expenditure, the answer is, yes.

On his own commission
as well?

No; not on his own
commission.

The minister should make an attempt to get from the contractors an approximate estimate of what they believe it will take to finish the building, and the time in which the work will be done, so that we shall not go on from year to year spending more money without any knowledge as to when we are going to be through or what the total cost will be. If it is a case of the architect making suggestions to the contractor and the contractor making suggestions to the architect for further expenditures, of course, it goes without saying that we shall never complete the building and these gentlemen will draw pay from the Dominion of Canada for the rest of their natural lives. The Government, so far, have not made any statement as to what additional fees they expect to pay the architect, or when he will finish making new plans for additions to the building.

I have already covered
the points raised by my hon. friend. I have given a rough estimate of the probable cost of the construction work that remains to be done, and I have also indicated approximately when it will be done. I was grieved to hear the hon. member's reflections on the architects and builders. I have been in fairly intimate touch with them during the past six months and I have an entirely different impression of them
both. I think the original Parliamentary Committee-of course, I was not on the committee and therefore cannot take any credit for what they did-made an excellent selection when they decided upon the present architects, and they made an equally excellent selection in Messrs. Lyall & Sons. As far as my observation goes, these gentlemen have all been satisfactory, and I do not think there has ever been any desire on the part of any of them to continue the work unnecessarily. They would all be glad to have the job finished and be about other more lucrative business. I am sure that is the feeling of the contractors and the architects.

Does the architect say
that he is practically paying out what he is receiving in the hire of other architects? Does he not get this amount for preparing the plans and looking after them, whereas the country pays for the supervision?

No, that is not the arrangement at all. The architect's duties are to draw the plans, oversee the construction, and see that the contractors carry out their work satisfactorily. What I did say was that the architect, in order to function properly, must have a very considerable staff about him, his own office staff. I am advised that at one time he had fifteen or sixteen employees in his office on his own pay roll, who must be paid out of whatever commission he would get on his work as architect of these buildings. What I pointed out before was, that these architect's fees were not personal payments to the architect but payment for the architect's services, which includes the services of his whole organization. It has been represented to me by the architect himself that if the architect's fees were to be limited to the fees on the original estimate of $5,000,000, he Would actually be out of pocket a large sum of money, instead of making a reasonable profit on the buildings, as he would in all fairness be entitled to.

Criticism of the buildings is a little out of place until they are entirely completed. The work is not yet finished. But it is not unusual for undertakings of this nature to receive considerable criticism. The party of hon. gentlemen opposite is the one that has always been prominent in decrying the efforts of this country to erect striking and noteworthy buildings. In this connection I wish to call the attention of the committee to a

certain historical document, a copy of which I hold in my hands. Everybody knows that the buildings which were destroyed by fire were very good buildings. But there is, no one who has had occasion to use the former buildings and compare them with the present structure but must come to the conclusion that the comparison is all in favour of the latter as regards beauty, accommodation, and interior arrangement are concerned. Now, the document I refer to was written by a gentleman named George Brown-Hon. George Brown to be perfectly accurate-in 1864, to Sir John A. Macdonald, at that time the Hon. John A. Macdonald, and it had reference to the former buildings, then under construction. After hearing this letter hon. gentlemen will come to the conclusion that history repeats itself, only the language used in 1864 was more mild and gentle than that which has been employed on the present occasion.
What is the date of the letter?

The letter reads as follows:
Toronto, August 15, 1S64.
My dear ISir,-MeDougair and' I made an examination' of the Ottawa buildings on Friday night, and we came to the conclusion that it was utterly impossible to take possession of the departmental buildings this Fall. By paying an enormous sum-say $715,000' to Sl'OO.OtO'O extra to the contractors-the thing might be done in December, but it would be at the risk otf the floors bursting up, and sickness to all who take possession of the rooms. What can be done is, to have the departments moved early in the year and Parliament summoned on the first of May, if that is thought to toe bettei than another session at Quebec; it is open foi adoption. But removal this fall would bring great discredit on us all.
I write all this very unwillingly. It would suit me vastly better to go at once to Ottawa, and I know how anxious you all are about it. but it was impossible to come to any other conclusion, after seeing the works and conversing with Mr. Page and the contractors.
The buildings are magnificent; the style, the extent, the site, the workmanship, are all surpassingly fine. But they are just 500 years in advance of the times. It will cost half the revenue of the province to light them and heat them and keep them clean. Such monstrous folly was never perpetrated in this world before. But as we are in for it, I do think the idea of stopping short of completion is out of the question. I go in for tower, rotunda, fountains, and every conceivable embellishment. If we are to be laughed at for our folly, at least let us not be ridiculed for a half-finished pile. I go in for making it a superb folly that will bring visitors from all countries to see a work they can't see elsewhere. To say the truth, there is nothing in London, Paris or Washington approaching to it.

The Governor General's residence is a miserable little house, and the grounds those of an ambitious country squire. To patch up that building will cost more than a new one, and 10 or 12 acres on the river ought to be taken into the grounds.
In haste,
Yours sincerely,
Geo. Brown.
Hon. J. A. Macdonald.
That letter was addressed to the Honourable, afterwards Sir John Macdonald, ir. 1864 When they were erecting the Parliament buildings which the party of my hon. friends opposite said were five hundred years in advance of the time. Now if those buildings were five hundred years in advance of the time, I would not be surprised if my hon. friends opposite were to say that the present buildings are a thousand years ahead of the time. I would commend the letter I have just read to the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill). I have had the honour of seeing a great number of magnificent buildings, but I do not think there are very many parliament buildings in the world which can compare with the buildings here; certainly there is not any in Great Britain or in Prance to compare with them. There may be at Washington, but the style of architecture there is very different. There are two buildings in Washington which may compare with the Ottawa buildings-one the Capitol building and the other the Library-but both are of different architecture. There is no gothic building in the world which compares in magnificence, size and architecture with the Ottawa buildings.

DIVORCE-ALPHONSE LeMOYNE DE MARTIGNY
House again in committee on Bill No. 120, for the relief of Alphonse LeMoyne de Martigny.-Mr. Ross.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When this Bill was last before the committee the preamble had been read, the consideration thereof had been postponed, and we were considering clause 1. Shall the clause carry?
Was it the same house in every case?

No, the woman and the
man lived in different houses. They lived in the same house, it is quite true, but there is no proof whatever that anything wrong ever took place between them. If anybody does say that anything of the kind took place he must take for granted something which was not proved in the case. From the judgment rendered by the Senate the inference apparently is

drawn that under the circumstances something improper must have occurred, and consequently the woman must have been guilty. I do not share that opinion, but even if that were true I would not take much interest in the fact as to whether the woman might be gitilty or not. I say that in cases like this a divorce should not be allowed. It should not be allowed because of the conduct of the husband. It should not be allowed because-

Mr. Chairman, I rise to
a point of order. I submit to the committee that, under a ruling made by this House four years ago in the Vineberg case, the decision of a committee such as the Private Bills Committee cannot be reviewed by this House, otherwise the usefulness of such committee would be at an end. The House must accept the decision of the committee which has dealt with the particular case to which my hon. friend refers; and the only course open to my hon. friend is to move that the Bill be referred back to that committee to take further evidence; he cannot argue, as he proposes to argue, that the committee did not come to a proper conclusion. If that were true, then every bill that is passed upon by the Private Bills Committee would be subject to review by the House and the committee practically would not function at all. I submit it is not open to my hon. friend to take the position that he does; he must accept the decision of the committee in this case, or move to refer the case back to take further evidence.

On the point of order I
wish to state that the questions of fact which were submitted to the Private Bills Committee, or the Senate, are questions which are pertinent to this committee to look into. I submit that we have a right to go into those questions of fact, examine them, and pass judgment upon them. If the opinion just given by the hon. member for Ottawa was well founded the decisions rendered by the Private Bills Committee, or by the Senate, on questions of fact, would be supreme. In that case it would be unnecessary for a bill such as this to be brought before the House as we would have to take it for granted that the moment the Senate, or the Private Bills Committee, had passed a bill the House had nothing more to do with it. I submit such is not the case.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the clause
carry?

No, I have not finished;
I was arguing the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Does any other hon.
gentleman desire to speak upon the point of order?

I think my hon. friend
from Joliette has given a good reason why the point of order should not be accepted by you, Mr. Chairman. The hon. gentleman who raised the point of order argues that instructions may be given to the Private Bills Committee to allow further evidence to be adduced, but that no argument can be brought forward in this House against the evidence that has already been heard by the Senate. Well, I respectfully submit that this is a mistake. An hon. member who wishes to move that instructions should be given to the Private Bills Committee to allow further evidence to be adduced must discuss the facts already presented in order to sustain his motion. I do not think, therefore, that the point of order can be maintained.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The point of order
raised by the hon. member for Ottawa is, that this committee has no right to review the evidence adduced before the Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and that the decision arrived at by that committee must be accepted, or the Bill be referred back for further consideration. I am sorry that I cannot sustain the point of order raised by the hon. member. If the committee of the whole House had no right to review the facts and the evidence there would certainly be no reason whatever for submitting the Bill to this committee, because a bill can only be referred back to any Select Standing Committee by the House itself. I have a distinct recollection that on more than one occasion a Bill of the same nature as that which is now before the committee was voted upon in com mittee and the different clauses of the Bill rejected after a very full discussion of the evidence adduced before the committee of the Senate, and this in spite of the fact that the bills had been favorably considered by the Committee on Private Bills.

Your decision, Mr. Chairman, being that this committee has the right to go into the evidence, I think if one reads the evidence carefully it will appear that it is very doubtful indeed whether the woman is culpable. Under the circumstances she should be allowed to have the benefit of the doubt; therefore we must take it for granted that in this case the wife is not guilty. Then the question arises: if she is not guilty, why did she not appear before the committee tc defend herself? Well, there are

several answers to that question. In the first instance, it may be said that she has already successfully defended herself before the courts of her province. In the second place, it is not very pleasant for a woman to appear before a committee and expose the facts relating to a case of this kind, and she might, therefore, choose not to appear. But the third, and, perhaps chief reason, might be that she is in collusion with her husband; that both are desirous that the divorce should be granted and she, not being guilty, would let her husband appear before the committee and contend that she was guilty in order that, to meet the desire of both, the divorce be granted. It is well known that no divorce can be granted in a case where collusion exists. In this particular case we have to come to one of two conclusions. Either the wife is not guilty, and for personal reasons she did not want to appear, or she did not want to appear because of collusion with her husband. In view of these facts, particularly in view of the fact that the culpability of the woman has not been proved or at least has been only very doubtfully established, I think that the divorce should not be granted.
But apart from the reasons concerning this particular case there are other general principles which enter into a consideration of the matter. We have no divorce law in Canada; consequently, there is no direction to guide Parliament in its decision to grant or not to grant divorces. In the province of Quebec we have a law which provides for separation from bed and board. That law declares that under certain circumstances the wife has the right to ask for separation from bed and board, and that under other circumstances the husband may apply for a like separation. When, therefore, there is a law defining the circumstances and conditions under which separation can be granted-and in this case I compare separation to divorce -the matter is made very much easier. But as I say, we have no divorce law and the only direction, if there be one, is in what I might call the unwritten law under which Parliament grants divorces. And what is the basis of that unwritten law? When the law is written the basis is the letter of the law, but in a case like this, where the law is unwritten, the basis is justice, honour, religion and conscience. The direction which Parliament must follow is indicated in these four words. I would be very careful in a case like this to avoid raising any question of race or religion, and I must point out that I am
pleading this question on the point of law and not on the point of race, religion or prejudice. On the point of law, then, I say that this is a case from the province of Quebec. It is a case in which Catholics are concerned, and I should hesitate to say that the principles which apply to Catholics in a matter of this kind should be set aside or not taken into account. When the case comes from Ontario, where the parties are Protestant, the law of that province and the religious principles of the parties must be taken into account. Similarly when the case comes from Quebec, the religion of the parties, the law of the province of Quebec and the conditions which exist there should be taken into account. However, I say this only en passant, because I think I can safely put my case on a more general basis; I think I can look at it from the broader point of view, although I would not like to pass over the point which I have just put forward. In a case like this, then, I can safely place on the same footing the Protestant minister and the Catholic priest, and I think I can invoke the principles of both the minister and the priest in contending that a divorce should not be granted in a case like this. We all acknowledge the sanctity of marriage; it has been recognized by all creeds, by all races, and at all times in the history of the world. We are all aware of the fact that Protestant ministers hold just as strong opinions against divorce as do Catholic priests.
Starting from the point that Parliament is supreme and that Parliament is called upon to pass an Act for the relief of Alphonse LeMoyne de Martigny, I ask: Is this a case where relief should be given? Is this a case where the plaintiff is entitled to relief? The plaintiff in this case is not entitled to relief because he does not deserve it. When a man has lost his wife, not through being guilty himself, when a man has been separated from his wife and the conduct of the wife has been bad, that man can come before Parliament and ask for relief, and Parliament in its wisdom will decide whether or not relief will be granted. In many cases relief will be granted where the husband deserves that relief; but in this particular case relief cannot be granted because the conduct of the husband is much worse than that of the wife, even assuming that her conduct has been bad, which has not been proven in the present case. When a man's conduct is that of this man, as was proven and declared before this committee, the last time the Bill was before the com-

4C06
mittee, and more particularly, as was pointed out by my hon. friend from Ka-mouraska (Mr. Stein), when the conduct of the man has been proven to be such as to be much worse in the present case than the conduct of the wife, even if the wife were guilty, I say that the man is not entitled to relief. What is he seeking relief for? The only relief which Parliament can give to him is relief from paying a pension of $125 a month to his wife and child. Surely he does not want relief to get married again, because, according to his own admission, he is living with another woman and, since he has been separated from his wife, he has been living with several other women. What relief does he want? He wants to get rid of his wife, to stop paying her $125 a month, and what is much worse, he wants to get rid of the moral and natural obligation of paying a pension to his child. That is the only relief which can be granted in the present case. The principle upon which I stand is that in every case where the husband is more guilty than the wife, he should not be granted relief. Before a man can come before Parliament and ask for relief, he must be guiltless of wrong doing. Then-and this is my last word- are we going to forget that through granting relief to this man, who does not deserve such relief, we are going to declare that the mother of this child is a bad woman? This young girl, twelve years of age, will be told in years to come, simply because Parliament wanted to grant relief to the father, which relief the father did not deserve, that her mother was a bad woman and that judgment to that effect was given by the Parliament of Canada.
Therefore, to summarise my opinion in a few words, I say: Taking into consideration all the circumstances, I submit the case has not been proven, or at all events the proof which has been offered is so doubtful that I would not pass judgment upon it and say that the wife is guilty. In the second place, I say: Even should the wife be guilty, the husband cannot ask for relief from Parliament because he himself is more guilty than his wife, and in a case like this where there is no written law upon which the husband can base his claim, no written direction to Parliament, Parliament in its wisdom and discretion and hy all the means in its power should say to this man that, until he has proven himself to have clean hands, he cannot come to Parliament and ask a divorce from his wife, simply because that will release him from paying a pension to his wife and 
child, which pension he is bound, by all laws of right and nature, to pay.

This is a very curious situation. We find a man, who is a French Canadian, getting a divorce through the Senate Committee, and all his compatriots in this House are opposed to his getting the relief for which he is asking. My hon. friend (Mr. Denis) proclaims the doctrine that because this man is a Roman Catholic, he should not get a divorce. I had an idea that the laws of this country granted to a Roman Catholic the same rights as to a Protestant.

I would not like my words to be distorted. I never said anything of the kind. I said, on the point of law, that we should not lose sight of the fact that these people are Catholic. I did not for a minute say that this point of law was supreme; that it should be the test of the case. I said that that was one consideration that should weigh in the balance.

That is advanced by the hon. member as the reason why this couple should not be granted a divorce. This man is entitled to the same rights and privileges as any other citizen in Canada, and I do not see how we can get away from that. He finds himself in this position; he finds himself required by a decree of the court to pay $100 a month alimony to his wife who, he declares,-and she does not deny it,-is living in adultery with another man and has been doing so for a number of years. That being the case, the man undoubtedly should be given relief, because only in this way can he accomplish two things. Only in this way he can escape payment of alimony to a woman who apparently does not deserve alimony, and as she has another man providing for her, why should he pay alimony? In the next case, if he is granted a divorce-
Where does the hon. gentleman see in the evidence that there is another man providing for the lady in question?
I do not think there is any doubt about that.
Where does he see that in the evidence?
That is the statement made.
By whom? It is a bare and unwarranted statement.

The other side of the question is this, that if this man is granted

a divorce, he is then in a position to get married and to live lawfully with a woman. He is entitled under the law of the country to get married again if this Bill goes through.
Never.

The hon. member says, "never". I quite understand that if the man remains a member of the Roman Catholic Church, he cannot do that. The law, however, of the church is one thing and the law of the State is another; but as regards granting a divorce and putting a man in a position to marry again, the law of the State is supreme. Whatever penalty the ecclesiastical authorities like to impose is entirely within their discretion-and I am not going to question their right to do that.
I do not see any reason in the world why the man's race or religion should debar him from having the same rights and privileges as any other citizen of Canada. The hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis), who ha3 just sat down, points out that by the laws of the province of Quebec a man can get separation, but that separation does not save him from paying alimony. To escape paying alimony and to undertake proper relations with some other woman, this man has to get a divorce, and I think he is entitled to that. The hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent), speaking on this question the other day, said that the woman had not been convicted of adultery, and he read part of the evidence taken at a trial in 1912 to prove that point. I submit that there was plenty of time between 1912 and the present day for this woman to be guilty.

If the hon. gentleman
will allow me to correct him, I said that in 1919 the same evidence was brought forward, and additional alimony was granted the lady in question. Is that sufficient for the hon. gentleman?

I would say that there
was still plenty of time between 1919 and 1921 for the woman to be guilty. An application for a divorce was made, and this woman was notified to appear and give her evidence in rebuttal of the most serious charge that can be laid against any woman, but she took no steps whatever to clear herself of the charge before the proper tribunal set up by this country. I do not think under the circumstances that we can assume that the woman is innocent. It would be an extraordinary thing if we could. If we are going to review the
evidence, we ought to have a divorce committee of this House. For us to refuse to accept the evidence that was presented by witnesses sworn before the Senate Divorce Committee, and then without re-examining the witnesses, to say that they did not tell the truth, that the facts are not as stated, and that we will therefore throw the Bill out, seems to me to be an extraordinary proceeding. I do not think there would be any justification for that at all.
The other ground stated the other day why this divorce should not be granted was that there was collusion. The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) argued that because he suspected collusion the Bill should be put over. Now, the Senate Committee was better able to decide that question than this House, because they had all the witnesses before them, and were able to examine them on that point as well as on any other point. Surely we are not going to say that the Senate Committee, which heard the evidence of these witnesses, is not in a better position to judge whether there was collusion than we are. I think it is an extraordinary thing that an attempt should be made to prevent this Bill going through when scores of Bills of this kind go through this House without any more or any less evidence of collusion than in this case.

Does the hon. member
know of any other case where evidence was offered before the Private Bills Committee with the view of contradicting the evidence taken by the Senate Divorce Committee?

No, but I say that the
gentleman who appeared before the Private Bills Committee did not appear for the woman.

Suppose he appeared
for the sake of society.

He did not come there
representing anybody but himself; he said so. I do not know that we should attach much weight to representations made in that way by a man who was not sworn, but who simply appeared before the committee to make a statement. He said that he was a relative, and that he had the interests of the child at heart. I do not think that his statement should take precedence over the sworn evidence taken by the Senate Divorce Committee.
I do not agree with the doctrine of the hon. member for Joliette, that this Parliament should act on the unwritten law rather than the written law. We have a method of getting divorce in this country,

and that method has been followed in this case. Everything has been properly done, the proper tribunal has given a decision, and now when the case comes to us, surely we are not going to go all over it again. If we attempt to do that, we must call the witnesses, and appoint a committee to hear the evidence that has already been taken by the Senate Committee. It is quite immaterial to me what happens to Mr. Martigny; I would not know him from a side of sole leather; but if we are going to have equality under the law, surely this man is entitled to the same consideration as scores of other men whose applications for divorce have been granted by this Parliament. It is perfectly absurd to say that because the man is a French Canadian he should not have the same rights as a British Canadian.
Who says that?
I am fighting for you fellows.

The question is not
whether this gentleman is entitled to equal rights with a British Canadian. We live under a constitution that gives equal rights to all Canadians and British subjects. The question is whether in the present instance the facts and the procedure justify the granting of a divorce. Divorce, like separation from bed and board, is always a very serious matter, as it affects the fundamental rights of the family and of society. The family is the basis of society, and if you destroy the family by the granting of divorce, or separation from bed and board, without scrutinizing very closely the facts of the case, you are not playing fair or doing the manly thing towards your conscience and towards society.
In the present case, I would call upon my hon. friend to read very closely the evidence which has been adduced in the other chamber, and as a gentleman who claims to be a Christian, as I do, he will find that the evidence does not justify the granting of a divorce in this case. If, as was stated the other day, in the courts of this land, where applications for separations are heard, the judges found that the facts did not justify granting a separation, I say there is much less ground for the committee of the Senate granting a divorce in this case. At all events, that is the business of that committee. But this House has also a committee, the Committee on Private Bills, and I think that we are entitled by jurisprudence to ask that

the evidence be heard before the Private Bills Committee.
I have said on another occasion that there has been collusion in this case, and I say now, there has been collusion. Further, Mr. Chairman, I object as a member of this House to being canvassed on such a serious matter as this or on any other matter coming before this Parliament, and there has been a systematized canvassing of members for the granting of this divorce. I object to the canvassing of members on any question, because members of Parliament must act as free agents; but if there should be objection in any one particular instance it is in the case of divorces. It is nothing short of a scandal that members should be button-holed and canvassed for the purpose of giving to a young lothario at large the divorce which he is sc anxious to secure. The evidence in the case does not justify the granting of the divorce. There is collusion in the case, and it seems to me that when this statement is made there should be no desire to rush the passage of the Bill. We are all sitting in this case as judges on the bench, and when a judge informs the court, first, that he has been canvassed, and secondly, that he can prove that there is collusion in the case, I do not see why his brother judges should say: "No, we must deal with the case as it is before us." I say, Mr. Chairman, that as a judge in this case I have been canvassed, and I have the evidence that there is collusion. Surely, then, the Parliament of this country will not lower itself to the point of granting a divorce under such circumstances. I will object strenuously to the passing of this Bill.

I am not a member of
the Private Bills Committee.

You are a member of
the House.

I am aware of that
fact, thank you. I am not a member of the Private Bills Committee and therefore no one would canvass me in regard to this or any other divorce case. Nor has any one done so. I have not read the evidence in this case, and was not present in the House when it was under consideration before. So that any conclusion I have drawn is based on what I have heard since eight o'clock. Now, in regard to the question of collusion-and my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) states positively that there was collusion-it strikes me as somewhat strange that hon. gentlemen who preceded the

member for Maisonneuve, on that side of the House, should try on behalf of the defendant to prevent this divorce going through. If, according to the hon. member for Maisonneuve, there was collusion, then undoubtedly the two parties would be agreed on the desirability of having the divorce go through; they would both want it to go through. I do not think that the question of the religion of the applicants for divorces is something that should be brought up in the House. I do not care what their religion may be, because whether or not a divorce should be granted to any applicant is a matter that should rest on a basis other than the respective religions of the parties. If the case has not been proved against the defendant then the divorce should not be granted. I understand that when the committee passes its opinion on a Bill like this it takes all these facts into consideration, and having done so reports to the House with a view to having its decision approved by the House. It is then the responsibility of members of Parliament, doing their duty in the case, to come to a conclusion as to whether or not the fact of adultery has been established against the woman. Those who think that the case has not been made out, according to the evidence submitted to the Committee, certainly 'should vote against the Bill; that is the only course open to them; and those who consider that the evidence is sufficient, and that the case has been established, must record their opinion the other way. ' One thing must strike every one as being a little strange in this matter,-I know it influences me in my judgment of the case,-and that is that this woman, who is within easy reach of Ottawa, has never tried to prove her innocence. She is charged before the Senate with having lived in adultery with this man, not in one house alone; whenever he moved she seemed to move also and live in the same house with him. As my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Hoeken) says, that is the gravest charge that can possibly be made against a woman; nevertheless, notwithstanding that the defendant in this case lives in proximity to Ottawa, she has not made any attempt to defend herself against that charge. That fact weighs with me, as it would in any other case, whether it were a divorce case or not. One is bound to be influenced by a fact of that kind. We had nothing in rebuttal of the statement made by the petitioner; no evidence has been adduced to contradict it. Under the circumstances I do not see what else the Private Bills Committee or the Senate could have done, on
such evidence as they had, than to recommend a divorce. I do not see that the Private Bills Committee could have done anything else than endorse the act of the Senate in passing the Bill on to this House. For the reasons I have stated I shall have to vote in favour of the granting of the divorce.
Before I conclude I might remark that this case furnishes another example to this House and to the country of the deplorable situation that exists in this country in the matter of divorce. We should have divorce courts in the Dominion of Canada. I have long been of that opinion, which I believe is shared by the vast majority of the people of the country. Applicants for divorce should not have to come before the Senate and the House of Commons but should have their cases tried by properly constituted courts established from one end of the country to the other.

I am sorry to have to address the House again on this subject as I did on Monday last, but, like several of my colleagues on this side of the House and even some hon. gentlemen on the other side, I feel that owing to lack of evidence in this case the Bill should not be accepted by this committee. Of course, I have the greatest respect for hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who do not share this opinion, and their position has been very frankly stated by the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). No doubt many other hon. gentlemen on the other side are in the same position as himself; they have not read the evidence. I believe that if hon. gentlemen did read the evidence carefully and, as I have done, several times, they would have no difficulty in concluding that there is not in this case that amount of evidence which is ordinarily brought before the Senate Committee on similar cases. As I stated the other day, I took the trouble to read the evidence in a few other divorce cases and I failed entirely to find any such lack of evidence in any other divorce proceedings as there is in the present case. The hon. member for Toronto alluded a few moments ago to the evidence that had been adduced before the courts of the province of Quebec in this case as far back as the year 1912. I may be allowed to correct some of his statements. The other day when I spoke on this matter I had not the exact dates before me; I have them to-day, however. The first time the case came before the courts of Quebec in the city of Montreal was in the year 1912, on November 22. There Mrs. de Martigny

instituted an action against her husband to obtain separation from bed and board, under our provincial law. She secured a judgment in 1912 and her husband was ordered to pay her a monthly allowance of $100. The matter remained in abeyance until 1919, when Mrs. de Martigny again came before the Montreal courts and asked that the monthly allowance of $100 be increased. Her husband contested her petition and also asked to be given the custody of the child, and in order to sustain his petition he alleged the very same facts as those alleged by him in his petition before the Senate Divorce Committee. The case was heard, both parties presented evidence, and two judgments were rendered on April 23, 1919, by Mr. Justice Duclos. He increased the allowance, rejected the petition of the husband to be given the custody of the child, and declared that the husband had not proved his allegation that it was not in the interest of the child that she should remain with her mother as previously, because he was openly living with another woman. The husband appealed against those judgments in the Court of Revision, and while that appeal was pending the husband's mothfer filed
9 a.m. an intervention in the case claiming the custody of her grandchild, stating that in her opinion neither parent deserved to have the custody of the child.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I am sorry to have to interrupt my hon. friend, but if he will refer to rule 25 he will find that Private Bills have precedence only for the first hour on Friday nights. It is now nine o'clock, and therefore I will be obliged to report progress on this Bill.
Progress reported.

The House again in Committee of Supply.
The Naval Service-to provide for the maintenance of the Royal Canadian Navy, $2,500,-
000.	I
Will the minister tell the committee what was done last year with the money then voted for the Naval Service?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. C. BALLANTYNE (Minister of the Naval Service) :
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I might first explain that I stated last year when the Naval Estimates were up that it was the intention of the Government to dispose of the Rainbow, the Niobe, and the two old

submarines, and that we had accepted from the Mother Country one modern cruiser, two modern torpedo destroyers, and two modern submarines. Those ships arrived at Halifax on December 18 last year, and at the present time they are on the Pacific coast. They will be leaving there shortly on their return to Halifax.
In answer to my hon. friend from Quebec East as to what we did with the money voted last year, we kept up the naval college, the naval dock at Halifax and Esquimalt, and we maintained in commission up to the time we sold them the Rainbow and the Niobe.
Who purchased the Niobe, at what price, and was the full price paid? Also, who purchased the Rainbow, at what price, and was the full price paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Niobe was
sold to the New Brunswick Rolling Mills Limited, after public tenders had been called for, for $135,000.
Was the full price paid?
Were many tenders put in?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I wish to slightly correct my statement. The New Brunswick Rolling Mills Limited bid of $135,000 included the Niobe and the two obsolete submarines. They have paid $20,000 so far on the purchase, and the balance is payable according to the terms of the contract. The following tenders were received for the Rainbow:
C. S. Sutherland Limited, Edmonton. $ 5.000
Yarrows, Limited, Vancouver..	. .	..	8,000
Alexander Zeeve, Seattle, Wash.. ..	34,565
Evans, Coleman & Evans, Limited,
Vancouver	 36,855
Nieder and Marcus, Seattle, Wash.. ..	67,777
The department accepted the highest tender of $67,777, and the money has been paid into the consolidated revenue fund.

Was it mentioned in the tenders for the sale of the Rainbow that only part of the purchase price need be paid, and time would be given for payment of the balance? My information is that it was a cash transaction, and some-

Louder, we
want to hear you down here.

I am asking the minister if when tenders were called for the purchase of the Niobe it was stipulated that it was to be a cash price. The minister has answered that part of the price of the successful tenderer was paid I should

like to know if it was not stipulated that the price was to be a cash price, because I have information from persons who did tender on a cash basis, and their tender was refused. Therefore, I think it is in the interest of the committee that we should know what the stipulations in the tenders were.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My information
is that no particular terms were specified in regard to payment. We simply offered for sale by public tender the Rainbow and the Niobe. Cash has been paid for the Rainbow, but only a partial payment of $20,000 has been made for the Niobe.

I think it is my duty to
point out that when these tenders were called for the Niobe-and that is the only ship I have any knowledge of-it was understood between the department and some persons in Ottawa who were prepared to purchase that ship that it was to be a cash transaction, and they were the highest tenderers on that basis. Now it appears that this New Brunswick firm was awarded the ship by simply paying $20,000. I should like to know if there is a binding contract with the New Brunswick company for the payment of the balance, when the payments are due, and whether the ship has been delivered to the purchasers or is still under the control of the department until the full purchase price is paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member is quite right that some tenders were sent in on a cash basis, but inasmuch as those tenders were all too low I refused to accept them and called for tenders on three different occasions. The tenders that we received were as follows:
John Simon, Halifax, N.S	 $20,000
J. E. Lipsitz Company, Chelsea, Mass. $80,000 Baker & Betcherman, Ottawa	 88,000
Those were cash offers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. The next
tenders were from:
J. E. I.ipsitz Company, Chelsea, Mass. $80,000 Baker & Betcherman, Ottawa	 88,000
We did not accept those tenders either because we thought they were too low, and for a third time we called for bids, with the following results:
Baker & Betcherman, Ottawa	$100,500
A. Carson & Co., St. John, N.B		112,000
Therefore we accepted later on the offer of the New Brunswick Rolling Mills Limited of $135,000, which included the two submarines, because their bid was a
good deal more than the highest bid of $112,000 from Messrs. A. Garson & Co. We gave them time to make their payments.

Were not the tenders of
$100,000 by the Ottawa firm and $112,000 by' the Halifax firm simply for the Niobe? Did these two tenderers understand that by making a further tender they would have to include the two submarines? And, further, what value did the department put on the two submarines that were thrown in to the successful New Brunswick tenderer at $135,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Even so, Mr. Chairman, if we deduct the price of the submarines the tender by the New Brunswick Rolling Mills Limited was still considerably higher than any of the other tenders.

Does the minister consider it was fair to ask tenders for the Niobe alone, and then, not having received sufficiently high tenders, to say to one company, without giving the others an opportunity to tender, "Oh, you may tender also upon two submarines"?
Was that the case?

That is the information I have. I should like to get an answer to my question as to whether the ship has been delivered to the purchaser or is still under the control of the department until the full purchase price is paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Niobe, I regret to say, is still at Halifax, and we may have some trouble with this firm. I have handed the matter over to the Department of Justice. But I am sure that all hon. members will at once see that after these bids came in, it was my duty, as the responsible minister, to accept the highest bid, and undoubtedly the bid of the New Brunswick Rolling Mills Limited was much higher than the next highest bid.

Of course it is the duty of the minister to accept the highest bid. But the minister has not yet made himself clear as to whether the two unsuccessful tenderers, namely, the Halifax firm and the Ottawa firm were made acquainted with the fact that the two submarines would also be included in the purchase price. My information is that they were simply asked to tender on the Niobe alone, which is an entirely different matter.
Would it not be good business in asking tenders to have it clearly understood what the terms are so as to prevent any misunderstanding?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am informed that the bids were on the same basis. All these tenderers were asked to bid for the Niobe and also for the submarines. Some of them bid for the Niobe alone, but the New Brunswick Rolling Mills Limited bid for the Niobe and for the submarines also. But if we deduct from the $135,000, $16,000 for the submarines, the price that we got from the Rolling Mills Limited for the Niobe was by far the highest price.

How does my hon.
friend arrive at $16,000 as the price for the submarines?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That was the highest bid we got for the two submarines.
Were there any separate tenders called for the submarines?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Tenders were
called for the Niobe as well as for the submarines. The highest bid for the submarines was $16,000.
Were there other bids for the submarines?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, quite a number of them. Messrs. A. Garson and Company, St. John, N.B., offered $6,500 for both-for CC-1, $3,000, and for ,CC-2, $3,500. Then John Simon, Halifax, quoted for the CC-1, $6,000, and the CC-2, $6,000.
How much was paid for these submarines?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: $1,100,000. We paid about $1,200,000 for the Niobe.

When the minister found that this New Brunswick company were able to pay only $20,000 on a purchase price of $135,000, did he take any security for the balance? Would it not have been better to accept the cash offer of $100,000 tendered by the Ottawa firm than to accept only $20,000 cash from another firm and then have to try to collect the balance through the Department of Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman would be quite correct in taking that ground if I had had any information before me at the time that the New Brunswick Rolling Mills were not able to pay for the Niobe. I have no reason now to believe that they are not able to pay. We did make careful inquiries with regard to the standing of the New Brunswick Rolling Mills, and the information was that their financial standing was good. Two bids were received, one for $88,000 and the

other for $112,000, and so far as I could tell both firms were in good financial standing. I am sure, therefore, that hon. members of the committee would have found serious fault with me if I had accepted the tender of $88,000 under those circumstances. The only reason why this firm has not taken delivery of the Niobe-and it is not a financial one, as I understand- it is that the value of steel and of everything that enters into the make-up of a ship like the Niobe has considerably depreciated, and this firm would now like to get out of their purchase. The Government, however, still have the Niobe. I do not know what other security we could take. The duty is now upon the Government of seeing that this firm carry out their bargain and pay for both the submarines and the Niobe.

Did
the minister take a cash deposit with the tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
Will the $20,000 be
forfeited to the Government if the contract is not carried out by the purchaser? If so, within what time will the money be forfeited?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not see any reason at all for letting this firm out. They knew what they were doing when they tendered for the Niobe and the submarines. Wc have $20,000 of their money, and we have the Niobe. The firm is financially good and it is the intention of the Government to see that they pay for the Niobe and the submarines according to the contract price, $135,000.
Was there a written contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
We ought to have it.

As I understand it, the minister thought the first tenders were too low, so he did not consider them. The third time tenders were called, a tender was received for $112,000 cash from a St. John firm and $135,000 cash from the St. John Rolling Mills, including the submarines. The law says that when tenders are called for the highest tenderer should get the contract according to the conditions of the tender. By what authority did the minister vary the conditions of the tender by allowing the New Brunswick Rolling Mills to pay the purchase price in instalments? Also, how were the instal-

merits to be paid and what was to be the rate of interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is true that this Ottawa firm quoted $88,000 cash; they did not want the submarines. The other tender was $135,000 but the tenderer in this case could not pay cash. I considered it was my plain duty to get the highest price I possibly could, and the arrangement was that this firm was to pay $20,000 cash and the balance at the rate of $10,000 a month.
What was the date of the contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am sorry I
have not the contract before me, but it would be in November or December of last year.
Have the submarines been delivered to this firm?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, but the Niobe is still at Halifax.

When the hon. gentleman says that the Niobe is still at Halifax, does he mean that the Niobe is the property of the Government? The fact of its being at Halifax or elsewhere does not necessarily mean that it belongs to the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Niobe is
being held at the port of Halifax until such time as the New Brunswick Rolling Mills carry out the terms of the contract. We are not going to turn over the boat to them until payments are made according to the contract.
The minister has said that the case of the New Brunswick firm is in the hands of the Department of Justice. What is the reason for its being in the hands of the Department of Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The reason is this: 810,000 was due from this firm on the first day of January of this year and $10,000 every month afterwards.
That is, according to the terms of the contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, and the payments have not been met. The only payment was the initial one of $20,000. The Department of Naval Service could not get the money out of them so we turned the matter over to the Department of Justice and told them to take the necessary steps to secure payment.
Have not the New Brunswick Rolling Mills paid for the submarines?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The total amount of their tender was $135,000. All that they have paid so far is $20,000.
Have they delivery of the submarines?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, but they have not delivery of the Niobe.

How
did the minister come to decide to deliver the submarines to the rolling mills without being paid for them? I understand that the $20,000 was a deposit which would be forfeited if they did not go on with the contract; that it was not part of the payment for the submarines. Do I understand the transaction to be that $20,000 was deposited as security along with the tenders; that it was held by the department for that purpose, and that subsequently the department turned over the submarines to this company without being paid anything for them?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The rolling mills deposited a cheque for $13,500 with us at the time they sent in their tender. This could not be considered a deposit cheque in the broad sense. They merely sent in their cheque for that amount to show their good faith.

Ten per cent on the
contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. We turned
over the submarines to them, and in addition to the $13,500 they made another payment of $7,000.

Was
that the price of the submarines?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, $16,000 was the price of the submarines. There is no question that the St. John Rolling Mills are trying to get out of their purchase; they are sorry that they put in so high a bid; they regret having bought the Niobe and *the submarines, and they are now trying to get out of their tender.
Have they been sued by the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When they defaulted on their payment, I at once sent an official letter to my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), enclosing a copy of the contract and asking him to see that the Government got payment or
else to take prompt action against this firm. I am not in a position to say how the matter stands at present.
Was this done a long time ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In February, if my memory serves me aright.

I cannot help thinking that the transaction as regards the submarines was unbusinesslike. The submarines, like the Niobe, should have been held until the Government were paid in full for these vessels. The fact is that the company made a deposit for the purpose of showing their good faith, that they would carry out their contract and purchase the boats when the Government delivered the boats to them, so that no part of that money should have been credited to the purchase of the submarines. They should have been paid for in full when delivered.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The company, at
the time the contract was signed, represented to the Naval Service Department that they particularly wanted the submarines before the bad weather set in. They said that they did not want to take delivery of the Niobe until later. From all the information that I had, they were good financially; I still think the St. John Rolling Mills are perfectly good financially, and we let them have the submarines. Our contract is a good contract in every way. There is no possible chance of the company getting out of it: the only way in which they could get out of it would be if they were in a position to implement the contract and pay for the Niobe. As far as I can learn, their financial standing is perfectly good, and we must see that we get our money.

Did the minister, after
getting the New Brunswick Rolling Mills to make this oifer to pay by instalments, summon the other tenderers and ask them if under the same conditions they had to pay, say $10,000 a month, they would not raise their tenders; or did he call for new tenders, stating in the notice that a certain amount of cash would be required and that so much time would be allowed for payment of the balance of the purchase price? I think that would have been a fair way to have handled the matter. If those men offered $135,000 for the submarines and the Niobe, took delivery of the submarines, got what they wanted and then turned their backs on the Government and said: "We will not carry out the balance of our contract," I do not think it is fair to say that

the deposit of 10 per cent should be credited to the payment of the submarines. If the same proposition had been made to the other tenderers, I do not say that that would have made any difference, but it would have been fairer and according to the spirit of the law that the minister should have called the others in and said to them: "Will you raise your tender if you are given time for the balance of the purchase price in addition to your deposit; or, if you deposit $20,000 on account, you can have the submarines, and we will hold the Niobe as security for the balance?" This firm probably wanted steel last fall, and when these two submarines which, I understand the minister to say, cost 'a little over $1,000,000, were delivered, and when this firm got the steel they wanted, as I said just now, they turned their backs on'the Government and said: "Now, look for the balance." They may be good financially; I do not know. I never heard of them before; I do not know the manager, nor the directors, nor who formed the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend has been a long time in public life, and ^ he knows that this is the usual practice. When public tenders are called for, as a rule they are called for only once. If I had followed the usual governmental practice, the minute these three tenders, namely, $20,000 $50,000 and $75,000 came * in, ^ I would have accepted the hightest bid, $75,000, and closed the transaction. No hon. gentleman would have offered any criticism in this committee at all if I had read out those bids and said that I had accepted the highest offer. It is an unusual thing to revise bids on three different occasions; but I considered the Niobe was worth a good deal more than the highest bid of $75,000 and, therefore, I worked diligently with those bids. This Ottawa firm, on the second bid, came up to $88,000; on the third bid they came up to $100,500. I do not think it would have made any difference in the price had we called these firms in and said:	"You need
not pay all cash; you may take a little longer time;" I do not think they would have changed their bids at all. If the department has made an error, the error has been made in endeavouring to get as high a price as possible for the Niobe

Having some knowledge of this matter in the way that I have mentioned, I must say that the minister wai insistent on getting a higher price than was offered by the Ottawa firm and by the

next lower tenderer at the time. He insisted that the price offered, by the Ottawa firm, even of $100,000 cash, was too small. My only criticism of the minister's action is that I think he ought to have acquainted the Ottawa firm and the Garson firm with the fact that they could make their payments by instalments. The offer of the Ottawa firm was a cash offer. They were told that they had to pay 10 per cent down and the balance the moment the contract was awarded to them. That was a specific declaration of policy on the part of the department. Now it seems that when the offers were refused, and properly refused because they were not high enough in the judgment of the minister, this New Brunswick firm was allowed to make a part payment, whereas the Ottawa firm and, no doubt, the Garson firm, if they had been acquainted with the fact that they would be allowed to make part payments and would be given time for the balance, might have tendered higher.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend think that his clients would have made a higher offer had we given them time?

I am inclined to say that they would, because I believe that they were prepared to go higher. It is not every firm in Ottawa that is able to raise $100,000 in ten days. This firm was a responsible firm. In face of the fall in price of the brass, steel and iron in these ships, the New Brunswick firm very properly
Most improperly.

-endeavoured to get out of the contract because it was going to mean a big loss to them. The tenders in the first instance were called for cash, fen per cent down and the balance on delivery. I must say in justice to the minister that he was most anxious to get the very top price, hoping, no doubt, as he did, that this New Brunswick firm would be able to pay the $135,000. As a matter of fact, they have put up only $20,000, and he is likely to have these ships on his hands again, but one cannot criticise that because the representations made by this New Brunswick firm no doubt were that they were financially able to carry out their contract.

Was any specific time arranged for as to when the balance of the purchase money was to be paid by this firm?
254J

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have just answered that.

When was the sale
made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Towards the latter part of December last.
Christmas time.

The intention of the
minister may have been very good, but I think the results are very bad. The results are that this firm have these two submarines and all the steel they want, and the minister has the Niobe tied up to the dock. Why? Because steel has depreciated and the value of the Niobe in consequence has gone down.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What difference does that make, may I ask my hon. friend?
It makes this difference. If you put the Niobe under the hammer to-day you would not get $20,000, and you would have sold these two submarines and the Niobe for less than $40,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I would ask my hon. friend a legal question. If a firm like this, which is good financially, buys the Niobe and thft submarines for $135,000 and signs a bona fide contract with the Dominion of Canada, what difference does it make whether steel goes up 50 per cent or goes down that much? The contract is legally binding, and we will see to it that we get just as good a lawyer as my hon. friend to make them pay for what they bought.

That is not a legal
question. This matter is a question of finance cn which my hon. friend ought to know much more than I do. I say that if the New Brunswick Rolling Mills are as good a firm as my hon. friend pretends they are, they ought to be able to raise $135,000 just as well as the clients of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp). His clients were able to put up $100,000 cash. My impression is, without going into this matter, that this firm may have no assets. The stockholders may have great names, but 'they may not be personally liable. If that is the case, and the firm has no assets, my hon. friend will have no security except the Niobe, and if he sells the Niobe for $10,000, he will be out $70,000 compared with what he could have got if the tender of the clients of my hon. friend from Ottawa had been accepted. The firm may be all right; I do not know what their assets are, or who the manager is, but

to the ordinary business man it would look like this: According to the statement of the minister the two submarines cost $1,000,000. Now, if they have depreciated 50 per cent, they would still be worth $500,000, and if they have depreciated even 90 per cent, they would be worth $100,000. To the ordinary business man it would look as if this firm was running away with at least $100,000 worth of property of the Government, and saying that they would not pay the balance due on the contract.
