I do not know how it looks to my hon. friend, but here is a reputable firm that is going to allow itself to be dragged before the courts to pay the balance of the purchase money. They have these two submarines, the value of which may have depreciated. I do not say they would bring much in the open market as vessels to be used for naval purposes, but still the steel was there.
Mr. I'RIPP: They were purchased for scrap and the steel and scrap have gone down in price

Yes, that is the reason why they do not want to take the Niobe. This firm is willing to be dragged before the courts, and the first impression of the ordinary man, who is not a financier but a poor country lawyer, is that the assets *of this firm cannot amount to much, the personal liability of the stockholders must be covered, and that is the reason why they are going to take the chance of the sheriff coming in.

I am a little jealous for the high standing of the First Lord of the Admiralty in the Canadian Government, and I intervene at this; stage in the hope that this debate has already gone far enough in the way of presenting him to the country as a dealer in old iron. I trust without wanting to dictate to my hon. friends, that we may now turn our attention for a while to this vote of $2,500,000 which this minister is asking for the Naval Service off Canada. I could not help wondering as the old-iron discussion was proceeding, how long it fwill be before these three vessels the minister gox last year from the British Government will be sold for old scrap iron in this way. If that is to be the main business of the minister, I should be very apprenhensive if there was any danger of another war coming on, because, after all, the defence of our coast would not be very much pro moted by the minister continually dealing in scrap iron. Can he tell us how these three vessels are getting on? He will

remember that last year I told him in a very friendly way, for he and I are the best of friends, that I thought the Admiralty in Britain had put one over on him in presenting him with i/nese three vessels. I suppose part of this $2,500,000 is to be spent in the upkeep of these vessels. I should like to know where this $2,500,000 is going. That is a lot of money in the present condition of the finances of this country. We had last year a national debt of $2,250,000,000, and so far as the national debt of the country is concerned, we have just added to that $100,000,000, making the national debt $2,350,000,000. Now if part of this ,$2,500,000 could be saved, it would help us a little in the face of this enormous debt that we have to deal with. I should like to know how the dock yards are, and how many naval officers we have in the .Inside Service at Ottawa. We used to get a look at the officers a year or so ago; we knew when we were passing them on the street, because they used to have a uniform, but I believe they are knocking around in mufti now. I do not know whether the minister is rather ashamed of the Naval Service, but if he would put them in long trousers, or wide trousers, with a little decoration, we would know them when we met them. As it is, we cannot count them because we do not know them when we see them. It might save time if my hon. friend would make a little statement as to how these three ships which he got so cheap, are getting on, how the naval college is getting on, how many naval students there are, how many naval officers we have in the Inside Service at Ottawa, and how the dock yards are.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to give my hon. friend any information I possibly can. I am glad to note that he has missed the blue uniform of the Royal Canadian navy on the streets. The only reason why he happened to see them in that well-known uniform a year or so ago was because the war was then on. During peace time at headquarters they 'are not permitted to wear their uniforms. The ships on the Pacific coast at present are the Aurora, two torpedo destroyers, the Patricia and the Patriot. The cruiser Aurora was built in 1914, is oil burning, and carries a complement of officers and men numbering 318. The two destroyers are oil burners built in 1916 and carry about 90 each of a personnel. The total number of officers and men on these three ships is something like 600. The college at

Esquimalt is still carried on. Forty-five cadets entered for the last term, and while I do not yet know the results, the reputation that the graduates have had ever since the college was established in 1911 has been a most commendable one. The course is excellent and our young Canadian officers have done well in the British navy, in which we have something like 38. We are going to continue the college on the same footing that has been maintained since 1911. The dockyards at Esquimalt have been closed down for nearly a year. There has not been very much work and we therefore closed them and let all the workmen out except the necessary few to look after the stores, and the watchmen to look after the works. The Halifax dockyards are being operated on very much reduced time and our staff there is necessarily a great deal smaller than it has been. The vote we are asking for of $2,500,000 is for the operation and maintenance of the cruisers and two torpedo destroyers, two submarines, the college and the dockyards at Esquimalt and Halifax. This vote of $2,500,000 is no higher than the amount we spent in pre-war times. While before the war we spent $1,700,000, when we come to estimate the increased cost of oil, coal, wages, provisions, etc., I am happy to say that the cost to the country to-day is not one cent more than it was then, and instead of having an inefficient, obsolete and small navy we have a highly efficient fleet which has made a splendid impression at Halifax and at the Pacific coast.
Would these ships be of any use if war unfortunately broke out now? The Niobe and the Rainbow were not when the last war broke out.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The ships we
have now are of the most modern type. The Aurora is armed with four and six-inch guns and also torpedoes and the destroyers are of the most modern type. We hope they will never be called upon to do anything in the way of active service, but if they are they can certainly take care of themselves.

The minister
says that a number of the cadets have gone into the Imperial fleet. That would almost look as if, up to now, we have not employed our own trained sailors on our own vessels. Has the minister a hope that in the near future he will be able to absorb the Canadian-trained young men in the Canadian navy, such as it is at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
As some of my
learned friends would say, that is rather a leading question. It has been the custom of the Canadian Government since the Naval Service Act was passed in 1911 to send a certain number of graduates each year to the Imperial navy for training. They are paid, of course, by the Dominion of Canada. We have 38 there at present, and as vacancies occur we have always this service of trained Canadian officers in the home fleet upon which to draw. Of the 34 officers now on the Aurora and other ships, all are Canadians with the exception of four. The commander of the Patriot is a young officer of Ottawa named Beer and the commander of the Patrician is a Halifax man by the na/ne of Jones. These officers are graduates of the Canadian Naval College who have passed through the British navy and are now on our ships.

I thank the
minister for his courtesy, and the otherwise full reply he has made; but no doubt because he failed to note one point he has not given me certain information I desire. I asked about the number of naval officers employed in the office in Ottawa, how many saw active service, and how many would be fit for active service in case of war.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I regret I overlooked that point. We have six officers at headquarters, all of whom are either Royal Canadian Naval men or men from the British navy.

In answer to the member for Red Deer the minister has given in detail the personnel of the crews of various vessels in the Canadian Navy. He has said nothing about the Sheerwater and the Algerine. Are they still in the service of the department? Will the minister also give some reason for the increase in the amount of this Estimate? Last year the amount was $2,000,000; for the current year it is $2,500,000. That is a large increase and I should have thought, in view of the decreased cost of commodities, the estimate would have been for less this year rather +han more.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Sheerwater
and the Algerine were not Canadian, but British ships. We never had to do with them. They were under our jurisdiction acting for the British Admiralty during the war and as soon as the war was over they went back. The member for Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) says that the vote shows an increase of half a million dollars. My hon. friend will remember that when the

naval discussion took place last year I said that the amount required was $2,500,000, and later in the session, when I brought down the Supplementary Estimates, I said we would reduce that amount to $2,000,000 because we would not be able to get the ships from England until welh on iii the year. On that account we were able to afford to take half a million less; but I made it quite clear that if the ships had been out here all of last year we should want the $2,500,000. I therefore ask for that amount now.

The minister has stated
that he does not know who compose the New Brunswick Rolling Mills Company. As the Minister of Customs (Mr. Wigmore) comes from that part of the country he might be able to tell us who are the shareholders and directors of the company, and what is their financial standing.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I cannot give that information. I am perfectly satisfied, however, that they are able to carry on and pay whatever balance is due by them.

What is the basis for
your satisfaction?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Well,-they carry on a large business. They are a reputable firm and I am quite satisfied are able to pay their bills.

Has the minister any
idea why they have not paid their monthly instalment?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: The price of iron has dropped in the meantime. I do not know anything about it further than that.

I would like to know
what action the Government has taken in the meantime. I understand the sale of the Niobe took place in the month of December last. What action has the Government taken to force this company to pay the balance of the price they agreed to pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot add anything more to what I have already stated, that the Naval Department promptly notified the Department of Justice. I will find out to-morrow just what 10 p.m. position the matter is in, and let my hon. friend know, but there is no doubt in my mind that the only . reason why this firm want to get out of their contract is that the price of steel and brass has gone down-

Surely you do not call it a reputable firm?

Mr. BALLANTYNE but that does not let them out of the tender. As my hon. friend from Three Rivers knows, as long as a firm is financially good the Government are perfectly safe. It matters not to us whether the value of steel or brass goes down. Where a firm is financially sound, and our contract is good it is the simplest question of law to know that there is nothing to stop the Government from getting their money.

I quite realize that but the fact remains that although this firm, or any other firm, might have been financially sound in the month of December last, owing to the changed conditions in the commercial world and the decrease in the price of materials that has taken place since, it might not be quite so sound to-day as it then was. I think the department would have been justified in taking prompt action to force payment. Perhaps the Minister of Justice will be able to tell us what action his department has taken, if any, at the instance of the Department of Marine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think a moment's reflection will make my hon. friend realize that it is quite impossible for me to go round with a knowledge of what proceedings have been taken in the numerous cases that have been dealt with by the department. I shall be very happy to obtain the information for the hon. member, but I have not come here this evening in the position to give it to him.

If nothing has been done since last December in the matter of trying to force these people to take over this ship, there must be some reason for it. The Minister of Marine is a business man, and I am sure that if a matter of the kind were presented to him in his own personal affairs he would very soon find out the reason why' nothing was done in a period of five or six months.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not know
why my hon. friend assumes that nothing has been done. I have stated a good many times, and I now state again, that the Naval Department acted promptly, and I have no reason to think that the Department of Justice did not also act promptly when the information was sent. But my colleague the Minister of Justice has a great many things to look after, and he cannot tell just now how many letters have been sent or the nature of the replies received. I would be very glad to supply my

hon. friend with that information to-morrow.

Perhaps I can tell the Minister of Marine what is happening. The question was asked in the House about three weeks ago, and we were then told that efforts of some kind or another were being made to get this company to see the error of its ways and take over the ship. Using a humane method, moral suasion, is just about as far as the department got,
I think.

My reason for asking the question was, that earlier in the session we had a similar discussion over another matter in connection with this department, the sale of an icebreaker. If my memory serves me rightly at the moment we were told this icebreaker was sold for a certain amount of money, but *on that occasion notes were taken, which notes were endorsed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We are on the Naval Estimates now.

I was explaining that
my reason for asking the question was that we had a similar occurrence before, and in that case the. department took notes which were endorsed.

The statement made by
the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Marine that this company is a firm of high standing is not substantiated by the facts. A firm of high standing will not repudiate a debt because the price of the commodity purchased is going down. As I said just now, it leaves the door open to suspicion, and the suspicion which naturally comes to one's mind is that this firm, the New Brunswick Rolling Mills, depend on the fact that they may have some political pull perhaps to get them out of the hole and they prefer this to the judgment of a court. I want to put things as they are, and I repeat that is the impression that remains in one's mind when we view the transactions from the beginning up to the present time, and when we cannot learn anything about the assets of the New Brunswick Rolling Mills, what they are doing, or anything about them. We are told they are a good firm, that they are an honourable firm, but I say that prima facie the fact of repudiating a debt does not inure to the credit of any firm or any company,, especially when the debt is repudiated after they have bad the best of the transaction- that is getting all the steel they wanted
when steel was high, and refusing to take the balance when the price went down.
Where is the Stadacona now?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Stadacona
is one of the fishery protection vessels, but is laid up at the present time because she is very costly to run, and the vote I am asking for to-night is not really sufficient to keep all the fishery protection vessels in service. We are laying up two on the Pacific coast and two on the Atlantic coast.
The Stadacona is resting then?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: She is resting.

To revert to this
Niobe transaction, I should like to ascertain from the minister why it was, when this New Brunswick firm failed to take over the boat, they did not offer her for sale again by tender as they did two or three times during the fall of 1920? The minister will remember that a certain client of mine made an offer, I think of $90,000, for that boat and we heard nothing about the fact that the boat was not taken over by the people who were fortunate enough to get her until Parliament met and the question was asked in the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will have to
answer that question by putting a question to my hon. friend: If he owned a private house and that house was bought, and he got $8,000 for it, and another man came along and offered him $15,000-the sale being good and all the papers legally correct -would my hon. friend take the house over?	.

I think in the case of a
falling market I would notify the party who had bought the boat that the boat would be sold at his cost and charge, and then sell it to the next highest bidder.

Before the item goes through I would like to make a remark or two about this business. I have no desire to obstruct the minister's Estimates, but I took the position in the House last year, the minister will remember, that we might very well at the present time hold our hand, and I expressed the fear that the minister had made a mistake in taking these vessels from the British Admiralty at this time. I pointed out to him the gravity of the toboggan slide at the top end of which he had entered, and his Estimate has gone up by a cool half-million this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, no.

I understood
there was a $500,000 increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not a cent.

I would be
glad to have that explained.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) asked that question a few moments ago. Last year I informed hon. gentlemen that the amount I desired voted for the Naval Service was two and a half million dollars. Later on in the session I informed the House that we could reduce that amount by half a million dollars, due to the fact that we were not going to get these ships out from England at as early a date as I had hoped we would. But I said then that if the ships had been out during the past fiscal year we would have required $2,500,000, and that we would require $2,500,000 for this year. The vote we are asking for this year is exactly the same as that for last year.

That statement is quite satisfactory, and I am glad to be advised that there is' no increase. But I cannot help feeling regret that at this particplar time those ships did not stay in England. Then we would not have needed $2,500,000 for a year or two. We do not feel any loss from the Stadacona taking a rest. There is not much difference between the minister and myself on some points, anyhow, because all I say is the Government should have taken a rest in regard to this business for a few years. No sentiment expressed in the House this session has received warmer commendation from all quarters in this country than the sentiment expressed by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) in his remarks in the debate on the Address that we might very well under the present circumstances of the world take a five years' naval holi-' day in Canada, and a considerable portion of a military holiday too. I know that defence is the first duty of the state, but I have argued on other occasions that when the time for defending the state came Canada was not lacking, she was there. And I am not at all sure that I have not misrepresented the Rainbow to-night, I am not at all sure that she did not do something at the beginning of the war, and if I have misrepresented her along that line I express my regret. But we were there as a nation, and we did wonders, and we did it all the better because we had not been
{Mr. M. Clark.]
spending too much money on military and naval establishments before. I only want to record my opinion that this is a melancholy business, we have gone into. Here is a story tonight of scrap iron-the minister to all intents and purposes so far as the Rainbow and the Niobe are concerned is a dealer in scrap iron. And he has another vessel now taking the rest cure, but I do not think it will ever do her any good, because she is 26 years old, and she cost a great deal more money when she was going than I hope she will cost while she is resting. It is said we should not look a gift horse in the mouth. Well, I would not have looked at the animal at all, and I regret that these vessels were accepted. I repeat, it is a melancholy business in view of the financial position of the country. It is between him and the Minister of Finance, and I hope they will take the matter into their very serious consideration and see if they cannot keep this business well in check. It ought to be easy, as we are all going into the League of Nations. Every member I have no doubt has received notice, as I have, to attend a meeting on Tuesday next to consider Canada entering into the League of Nations. We have come out of a war of unparalleled magnitude in which we suffered terribly along with the other belligerent nations, and we were told all along that that war was to end war, but here we are again with a militant First Lord of the Admiralty with fire in his eye leading us on to this business of armaments. I can only express my regret that what I said to the minister last year has done no good, although he has had twelve months to reflect, and I can only hone that in the next twelve months-if he is so long in office- he will mend his wavs and get some information that will lead him to substantially moderate this business.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend
had his full share in the naval vote of $2,500,000, and all hon^gentlemen opposite also had their full share in it. I find no fault with them whatsoever for that. Canada under the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier decided to have a navy of its own. The Naval Service Act was passed in 1911, my hon. friend was a member of the Liberal party at that time, and the Government of the day decided that we would look after our own naval defence.
Let me say again that I found no fault with the policy then, and I find no fault with it now. The Naval Service Act meant this. The Government of the day

said to the Home Government, "Take away your ships and no longer look alter the dockyards at Halifax and Esquimalt. Canada will assume that responsibility." And that responsibility is on this Parliament to carry out the terms of the Naval Service Act, which my hon. friend had his full share in passing in 1911. The Niobe and the Rainbow were brought out from England with the approval of my hon. friend. Now he would have been perfectly satisfied had we continued with those two vessels.	<

As training
vessels.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The vote would
have been exactly the same as it is now, $2,500,000. We are carrying out the policy of the hon. member for Red Deer and of the Government of that day which he supported, and we are not increasing the expenditure one iota. What has this Government done? We have discharged 783 civilians and naval ratings that we did not need, we have sold those obsolete ships, and we have accepted modern ships as a free gift from the Mother Country. My hon. friend says it is a melancholy vote. Yet if anybody ought to appear in sackcloth and ashes it is my hon. friend from Red Deer. He helped to put the Naval Service Act on the statute book, he gave his consent that Canada was big enough and strong enough to take over the docks at Esquimalt, to support a naval college, and to bring out the Niobe and the Rainbow. The policy followed since the passing of the Naval Service Act must be the policy of Canada until such time as that Act is amended or repealed. My hon. friend took that responsibility; I think he took it rightly; but he cannot get out of it now by attempting to shift the responsibility on to me, although never at any time am I afraid to take my full share of that responsibility. Had we not accepted these ships from the Mother Country we would have had a disgracefully inefficient Naval Service, a service not worth one cent to Canada, and the expenditure would be just the same as we have now for a very efficient navy.

I am sorry
my hon. friend has made such a combative statement in response to the very peaceful speech on my part. I do not propose to follow his example; I am going to keep to the peaceful frame of mind in which I talked to my hon. friend before. If he has not had enough of war I have, and I will not be tempted into strife by his very
combative mood. - He said the dockyards were taken over by Canada. But when he was on his feet a few minutes ago did he not say that those dockyards were practically closed down and he was getting his repairs done by tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

What did
my hon. friend say in his previous utterance about the dockyards?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Under the terms
of the Naval Service Act we have got to keep the dockyards in sufficient working order to repair any British admiralty ships that may require repairs. We have practically closed down the dockyard at Esquimalt, but we are keeping sufficient men there to attend to any needs either of a British naval ship or of one of our own ships. We are keeping the Halifax yard going with a very much reduced staff. In fact, both yards are being continued in a very moderate way.

I cannot
quite understand how a dock can be "practically closed down" and yet be "in sufficient working order" to do repairs. I am informed, it may be mistakenly, that repairs have been done by tender elsewhere, and that the dockyards are, as the minister says, practically closed down. If you have docks practically closed down, they are not fit to conduct business if language has any meaning. However, I will leave that point and pass on to the other portion of my hon. friend's argument. Now, I quite admit that he is pursuing a policy which was the acknowledged policy of a certain party in the country in 1911. He had had to train the party with which ho is now associating up to the point at which the Liberal party had arrived at that period

if we are to have a naval policy at all it is evident that ten years have sufficed to teach something on this question to the party on the other side. But I did not want to labour that point. I did want to point out to my hon. friend that there is no inconsistency whatsoever in my having supported that policy at that time as the only possible and proper naval policy for Canada and in my saying, after the war, when another war in which we should be involved is to all human thinking considerably remote: Go easy with your naval policy. I am wholly in favour of Canada as a nation undertaking her own defence; there is no inconsistency whatever in that attitude on my part. But the minister is inconsistent in going full

steam ahead after a war just as he would have been going before the war-that is my answer to my hon. friend on that point. However, I do not want to be drawn into a controversy; I have made my protest, and I want to express my very grave fear that, unless he changes his politcal affiliations once more, it will not be the present Minister of Marine who will be dealing in the scrap iron but somebody else if we go on with this business. After all is said and done, Mr'. Chairman, I would rather that the business of the Admiralty was confined to getting presents of vessels, scrapping them and selling them as old iron than that we should be in another war. I do not change my point of view, however, that we might very well have waited in the present circumstances, as I suggested last year, until an Imperial Conference should settle upon proper lines the question as to what each part of the Empire should do for the defence of the Empire.

I think the minister is to be congratulated upon having cut down the ratings for the navy to the extent that he has. But I feel that it was a great mistake to take these ships from Great Britain. It was done while Parliament was not sitting; it was done without consultation with the representatives of the people, and it puts us in the awkward and unpleasant position of appearing to be ungrateful for a free gift. I do think that the minister has placed the representatives of the people in an unfortunate position. Now, the minister has argued that the Liberal policy is responsible for the Laurier naval policy. I admit that most frankly. At that time the world was busy arming for what proved to be, alas, an awful conflict. We were told there was a great European power which was marching on and on and that at some time we would have to meet that power. Unfortunately the prophets of evil spoke truly. War did break out; the navy of that great power is to-day at the bottom of the North Sea, and for the time being, at least, that menace is no more. Under these circumstances would it not be the part of prudence to take a naval holiday? The desires and hopes and prayers of all men of good-will throughout the civilized world are centred upon the League of Nations. We are hopeful that through that body mankind will be able to develop a method of settling international disputes. Is it not, then, the height of folly to go on in the same way in regard to naval matters? Is it not unwise to contribute

$200,000 to the expenses of the League of Nations and then spend ten times that amount on preparing something which, if the League of Nations is a success, will in all probability never be required? The Laurier naval policy was proposed when our national debt was but $350,000,000; today it is $2,350,000,000. The minister therefore would confer a great benefit on the country if he would turn the prows of these three ships eastward and allow the Canadian people to see the smoke ascending from their funnels as they made their way home to the land beyond the seas. We cannot afford this expenditure at this time. We should not spend one cent except for absolute necessities and this is not an absolute necessity. I can hardly trust that the minister will change his view, but I would like to register my emphatic protest against this expenditure.
He is at sea on it.

Yes. We are here tonight knowing nothing more than the man in the moon about the sale of the Niobe and the submarines except that $135,000 was the price. We know that there is a default. We do not know how great the debt is. We do not know how the debtor stands financially. It looks, as my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) has said, as if the Dominion had been stuck for a very large sum' in this matter. We shall be told:
K We have the Niobe yet." That is true; but prices have fallen and we could not get for her now what we could have got before, and as a consequence the country is the loser.

The minister gave
the committee a piece of history which was somewhat incomplete. I would not like to supplement it in any way except to point out one feature in connection with it. When the naval law was adopted in 1910, the hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) who afterwards became Prime Minister of Canada, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) and all the other hon. gentlemen with whom my hon. friend is now associated, voted against that law and in favour of an amendment offered by the late Mr. Monk, that no naval policy should be adopted by Canada without being first approved by the Canadian
people. This issue was fought during the campaign of 1911. As a matter of fact in my province, it was the only issue discussed on the platforms. Twenty-six members were elected in the province of Quebec against that law and after the elections, when those people got together, after having accomplished what they had in view, they pledged themselves in Parliament that no permanent naval policy should be entered into by this country without being first approved by the Canadian people. The Prime Minister of that day took that pledge; the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the Hon. Mr. Hazen, stated it emphatically on the floor of the House of Commons, and I ask my hon. friends when the Canadian people have since then approved the present policy of the Government as regards the navy. As the hon member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) stated, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Government accepted those ships as part of their permanent policy, without asking the approval, not only of the Canadian people, but of the Canadian Parliament. This was done by Order in Council, of course, under the general practice of this Government at that time. Parliament was not consulted, and when my hon. friend came to Parliament with a proposed appropriation, we were faced by an accomplished fact. The ships had, been accepted, and we had to vote the money although we opposed the vote at that time. I was opposed to that vote being accepted; I am still opposed to it, for many reasons, one of them being, that there is no settled naval policy at the present time for the British Dominions. There is going to be an Imperial Conference next year. There is going to be a meeting of Prime Ministers this year. The name has been changed for the conference that takes place in July, and conditions are such that our Prime Minister stated the other day, or at least intimated in some way, that he would be opposed to the consideration of any naval policy at that conference next summer. Why should we not wait until the status of the Dominions is fixed, as we are told it is going to be at this Imperial Conference next year, before accepting, or adopting, any policy as regards naval defence? Conditions are altogether changed as the hon. member for Brome stated. In 1910, the country was prosperous; we had money; we had no deficits, we were not paying the rate of interest that we are paying now on our loans. We had not two billion dollars of

net debt as we have at the present time. Conditions are altogether changed, and as the hon. member for Brome and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) stated, we are paying an annual contribution to the League of Nations. We are members of that league. The last war was fought for the purpose of ending all wars. We should at least follow the example of those nations which are decreasing their armaments instead of increasing ours or entering into any new scheme. Last year there was in the Estimates a vote of $300,000 for the maintenance of the Canadian navy. That was the usual vote as in preceding years.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

There were two votes yast year: Naval Service, to provide for the maintenance of the Royal Canadian Navy, $300,000, and then in the Supplementary Estimates, there was the other vote: Further amount required, $5,700,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member will recall that I explained, when I asked for the $300,000 appropriation, that that was only part of the naval expenditure and that in the Supplementary Estimates I would bring down a further amount, so that he has to consider both of them together.
Yes, but this $300,000 vote was practically the same as the vote of preceding years during the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
What was the vote in 1919?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have the
amounts for all the years here. Before this is turned up, I might say that the expenditure was $1,700,000 in 1910-11. Then when we got into the war, of course, the expenditure ran away up, and it would not be a fair comparison at all.
The minister cannot tell me what the expenditure was in 1919.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will tell my hon. friend just as soon as my deputy arrives. He has gone upstairs for a moment.

Perhaps the deputy
would ascertain the names of this rolling mill firm while he is up stairs, and the minister could give us the information to-night, and also any information he has as to the firm's solvency.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will have to take the word of the [Mr. I.apointe.l
Government. I have had a very long experience in business, and I am sure my hon. friend has also had a very considerable business experience. He knows that before an ordinary business concern give credit, they look up the reports of one of the mercantile agencies, either Dun's or Bradstreet's, and if the reports of these 'agencies show that the firm's credit is good, business men do not ask the firm what their assets and liabilities are. They largely go by what their salesmen say, and also by the financial reports from these agencies. I took all these precautions at the time, but in these days, of course, when business is declining rapidly, a firm that may have been good a year ago may not be good now. From all I can learn, however, the firm is good. My hon. friend will have to take my word for it that at the time we made all necessary inquiries as to the firm's standing, and I was satisfied that they were good. The Government have to take financial risks, of course, just the same as any other concern.

Dun's and Bradstreet's reports show in detail what the concern is, what its products are, what its bonded indebtedness is, and all the details that we would like to have to-night; so, if this information is available on file, I do not think it would be a difficult matter for the minister to give it to the committee tonight, instead of saying that he got the information but does not remember now what it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh yes, I do.

Except that the firm was good. Well, it turns out that they are not good. If they were good, they would not be willing to have their reputation risked by being sued by the Government of Canada for this liability. They could not possibly stand that if they were good, because it would wreck the reputation of any solvent concern. If they were good they would not dare to assume the risk of having their credit ruined by refusing to pay a debt which the minister says is now due and owing.
In addition to that, as was pointed out by another hon. member, as soon as the responsibility was shifted from the Naval Department to the Justice Department, no further inquiries were made by the Naval Department to ascertain what was being done or whether the Justice Department had left the matter in the hands of some other official who was also taking a rest cure. This liability has been left standing for months, nothing has been

done, and we are not able to ascertain now whether this concern is solvent or not. Only the hope is expressed that they will pay the debt, and we are told that the Justice Department has been applying moral suasion in different doses for the last few months.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can now give my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) the information he asked for. The naval expenditure for the year 19101911 was $1,719,017; 1911-1912, $1,233,456; 1912-1913, $1,085,660. Then we got into the war years, and the expenditures were very large. If my hon. friend wants the figures for those years, I can give them.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There were small expenditures running up to about $300,000 or $400,000 for the upkeep of the Naval College and thing of that kind, but millions were spent which were charged to the War Appropriation.

I would judge that in the ordinary course of business, when this firm failed to make their payments as they fell due, the department would get into correspondence with them, and at least make some inquiry as to why they did not pay. Has the department done that, and if so, what answer did this firm make? Did they question the validity of the contract in any way?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Immediately they failed to make their first payment under the contract, my department wrote them, and followed the matter up for a considerable time. We did not get any satisfactory answer from the New Brunswick Rolling Mills at all; so, after following the matter up for a reasonable time, we turned it over to the Justice Department, and told them to take proceedings against the firm.
My hon. friend says that he did not receive any satisfactory answer. I presume that he received some sort of answer. What answer did they make?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot recall the exact phraseology now, but they were trying to get out of the contract owing to the market price of steel and brass having gone down very considerably.
Is that the only reason they advance?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is all.

They did not advance
that as a reason, did they?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They were trying to get out of the contract. They were trying to work the Naval Department to see if we were easy and would let them out of the contract, which we certainly will not do.

What was the nature of the instructions which the minister gave to the Justice Department? Were the instructions to sue for an instalment or for the whole amount? Was there any provision in the contract that the full amount would fall due if default was made on one instalment?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have no knowledge of law, but I should think that the only proceedings which the Justice Department could take against the firm would be to insist upon payments as they became due under the contract.

It is a very common provision in a contract of this kind, that if default is made in payment of one instalment the whole amount becomes due at once. I simply want to know if the minister had that provision in this contract?
I would suggest to the minister, if it can readily be done, that this correspondence with the firm be placed before the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have no objection at all.
Why did not the department insist that cash should be paid for this boat, instead of selling it on the instalment plan.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I know my hon.
friend did the best he could for his friends, and it may turn out that it would have been better had the department accepted the next lowest bid for cash, but as there was such a difference in the tenders I made the best deal that I could with this concern, after satisfying myself that they were financially good. I do not think I would have been justified in turning their bid down and accepting another bid some ,125,000 lower.

I asked the minister a question, but he did not answer me. I want to know what instructions he gave to the Department of Justice. Were the instructions to sue for $10,000 or for the whole amount? Has the minister received any report from the Justice Department on the contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I merely sent the tender to the Justice Department and ad-

vised them of the steps we had taken, quite unsuccessfully, to get the firm to meet their payments. A layman like myself would not presume to suggest to my colleague what legal steps he should take.

I must remind the
minister that twenty minutes ago he told us in the most positive way, in a way that no lawyer would dare to do, that the contract was absolutely good, perfectly sound, and enforceable in every particular. Now, when it suits him to say that he does not know anything about law, he tells us that he does not know whether the contract is good or not. The minister ought to be able to tell us what the terms of the contract were. I do not think that fhe tender was ever handed over to the Justice Department. The minister would naturally hand over what was finally consummated in the shape of a contract and which I presume is in writing. The preliminary communings that took place before the final contract do not cut any ice; the contract must speak for itself. The minister must surely have contemplated some discussion of this kind to-night and should have had the contract here. It would not take long for him to get it and we should like to see it. We want to know whose names are on it. It has been suggested to-night that some favoritism has been shown in this matter. Three or four persons tendered and all except one said that they would pay cash in full. This concern is not paying cash and some inside arrangements seem to have been made to favour them. They fell down on their contract altogether and yet are given five or six months' leeway without anything being done. That looks like favouritism. At all events it is what the minister would do for his best friend if he could do anything at all for him. He would say to his very best friend, political or otherwise: "I will turn down the cash tenders of the other people and take advantage of the fact that yours is a little larger, and I will give you the best terms possible and deliver the property to you. If you do fail in your payments I will give you all the time you want and go through the camouflage of handing the matter over to the Justice Department. But you need not be afraid of this; nothing will be done.'" That is what the minister would do for me if I were his very best friend. It remains for him to show that no favouritism characterized this transaction, but that on the contrary, it was a hard and fast business deal. He can make this point clear by

producing the contract and showing that everything has been open andi above board and done in good business shape. And he should do that before the item passes. We ought to have the contract, because this is something that the minister might very well have anticipated.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member will certainly see the contract to-morrow. I do not find any fault with him for imagining anything he likes. The transaction was a perfectly sound and legitimate business transaction and was perfectly above board. If I had accepted the lowest cash bid of $88,000 and someone had asked the hon. member to inquire of me why I had not accepted the offer of the St. John Rolling Mills at $135,000 even if the terms were longer, I could understand that the hon. member might possibly have something to say. But the whole criticism to-night is directed at the department because we did not take the lower tender, for the reason that it was cash, notwithstanding that it was $30,000 less. Possibly it might have been better had we taken it, although I do not hold that opinion. But everything was done in a proper way and I shall have no hesitation in bringing down all the correspondence, laying all the tenders on the Table, and producing a copy of the contract or the original itself. The Department of Justice was furnished with the contract which we entered into, and I have absolutely nothing to hold back.

Personally I do not propose to hold any post mortem upon this item. If we are to have any evidence on the matter at all we should have it before we pass the item. The minister cannot claim any credit for getting $135,000 instead of $112,000, unless he can show us that he is dealing with reliable people. To put up a straw company, such as this ap pears to be, which is not able to meet its responsibilities, which squeals because the nrice of steel has gone down, and which refuses to pay, is something for which the 'unister cannot take credit. There is no credit at all to him in the fact that he turned down a cash offer of $112,000 and accepted a vague promise of $135,000.
The minister had an offer of $112,000 from A. Garson & Company of St. John for the Niobe alone, and he threw in two torpedo boats, the CC-1 and the CC-2 and got $135,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I did not throw
them in at all.
They were thrown in.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, they were not. Let us be perfectly fair to one another;
I am fair to hon. members and they must be fair to me. I gave all the tenders that my department received for the submarines and I also gave all the tenders that we received for the Niobe. The highest third bid for the Niobe was $112,000, but we actually sold her for $119,000, apart from the submarines altogether. As regards the submarines we received from the St. John Rolling Mills Company the highest price offered by any firm. There is no case of throwing in the submarines at all. It was a straight case of calling for public tenders and giving the contract to the highest bidder. I know very well that these firms that tendered and did not get the contract were sorry; whether or not they are sorry now I do not know. Possibly they are behind all this questioning at the present time. What position should I be in as Minister of Naval-Service if after calling for tenders three times I repudiated the highest tender and gave the contract to another? I should not like to appear before the members of the committee under such circumstances.

The offer of $112,000
from Garson & Company was a cash offer, while the offer from the New Brunswick Rolling Mills of $119,000 was credit. That is the distinction.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend is
getting on to ground that he is not familiar with. It is hardly fair for me to express any adverse opinions regarding any firms that tendered, but it might interest my hon. friend to know that, as regards the firm that tendered $112,000, their cheque was returned to us as being no good.

The minister says
that this is a good company. He tells us that there is no doubt about its being solvent, and he is proud of the business deal he has put through. If that is so, surely the Minister of Customs can give us the names of the president and the general manager of the company. St. John is not so large a city. I know that if it were a Quebec company, and if the firm were a reliable one, as the minister says this is, I could give the names of the president and general manager. There is something queer about the whole matter. Surely my hon. friend can give us these names; and we are entitled to see the contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I have not been in
St. John since Christmas. I know that at
that time this firm were doing a good business. They were working day and night running a rolling mill formerly owned by the St. John Rolling Mill Company. The firm in question took over the St. John Rolling Mill and called it the New Brunswick Rolling Mill and since that time they have been rolling iron there. I know nothing about the business since January, but I can say that they were doing a good business at that time and that they are perfectly able to carry on and pay any indebtedness that they owe. Personally I think this contract is a good one from the Government's standpoint. If I understand the figures correctly, this company agreed to pay $135,000 for the Niobe and the two submarines.
But they did not pay it.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: The highest price received for the submarines was $6,000 each, making $12,000 in all. Take that from .the $135,000. The minister tells me that the amount for the Niobe was $119,000. Now, the manager of the firm is H. J. Garson and the secretary is a man named S. S. Elliot. Both are respectable citizens and good business men of the city of St. John, and I believe they are carrying on a satisfactory business.
Might I point out to the minister that this very Garson is the man whose cheque was returned?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: He is another Garson altogether.

A Garson of another
colour.

I do not desire to question the frankness of the statement by the minister in any way, but it does seem to- me almost incredible that a firm that is presumably composed of reputable business men would attempt to escape a straight unqualified obligation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, it is very
common.
It is common?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Common in business.

I am sorry that has been the business experience of the minister. I should say that reputable men
11 p.m. do not do that sort of thing. But what I was leading up to is this: There is just the suspicion of a feeling in my mind that the tender made by

that firm had in it some sort of qualifying clause, and it is on the strength of that possibly they are refusing to pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I can certainly
say most positively to my hon. friend that there is no qualifying clause in it at all, and from over thirty years experience' in business I can say that n'ot all firms by any means but very often very good reliable firms, when the market goes against them, do try to get out of contracts. It has happened to me many a time.
Do they merely default in payment, or do they allege any reason for not making payment?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Default only.
Have they taken delivery of the submarines?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
I understood the minister to say that he had an oifer of $100,500 from an Ottawa firm, and an offer of $112,000 from another firm and that those offers were on a cash basis?	'

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
I would like to ask the minister if he offered to sell the Niobe to those two firms on the terms basis which he made with the St. John company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The firm that
quoted $112,000 were not financially good, as I have already stated. The Ottawa firm that made the offer of $100,500 were good as far as I could tell at the time but the difference of $19,000 between that offer and the one accepted was so great that I did not think any good purpose would be served by going to them, after I had asked them to bid on three different occasions, and saying "Will you bid a fourth time provided I do not ask you to pay cash?"

How did the minister
arrive at the conclusion that it was good business to go to some other person with an offer after he had made three attempts to sell for cash? He had attempted to sell for cash but could not get a satisfactory price and he then accepted an offer on terms.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The only mistake I made, was calling for tenders three times.
I should only have called for tenders once.
I should have accepted the price of $75,000 and we never would have heard a word about it. The mistake I made, in my earnestness, was trying to get too much
	.
money for these ships. If I call for tenders again, after the experience I am having here to-night, I will award the contract to the highest bidder; I will try no more dickering.

That is one good reason why my hon. friend should not be in the position he is in, if he is going to get peeved because he is criticized for making a bad bargain and say that in future he is going to take anything he can get from the first bidder. If that is my hon. friend's intention he is in the wrong place when he is in a public office in this country; and it would certainly be in the public interest if he were to desist from making any more contracts for Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He will keep on.

He should attend to his,
private business and the country can get along very well without him if that is the attitude he is going to adopt. The minister called for tenders three times and in each case a greater amount was offered than in the case of the previous tenders. Why did he not call for tenders a fourth time when, perhaps, even more money would have been offered? But when he desisted from doing that and started to deal privately with this firm, why did he not deal privately with the other people who had tendered on a different basis? He says the man who offered him $112,000 was no good. Well, we have had evidence to-night that the company whose offer was accepted is not very good. Had the minister accepted the tender of $100,500 he would have been much better off. I cannot understand why he did not ask that firm for a better price provided he gave them time.

The minister fails
altogether to appreciate whatever criticism has been directed against him from this side if he imagines that we find fault with him for trying to get the best possible price. He is to be congratulated upon the fact that he endeavoured to get the best possible price. As I see it the only grounds for criticism are these: First, that having asked for cash prices he made a contract with one of the tenderers for a price which was partly in cash and partly on time without giving the other tenderers the same opportunity. That, it seems to me, may have operated unfairly. I do not say it did operate unfairly, but there was a possibility of unfairness there. The second ground for criticism is that having turned this collection over to the Department of Jus-

tice, he has not followed it up as I think a business man should have followed up the collection of such a very substantial amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
What makes my
hon. friend think I did not follow it up?

Because had the minister followed it up he would have told us that he had done so, that he had asked the Minister of Justice, or the Department of Justice to give him information, and he would have had some information to give to the committee. Now, we are almost in the month of June. I understand that the payment in regard to this contract was to be so much in cash and then instalments of $10,000 a month, beginning with January 1. Well, there are the instalments for January, February, March, April and May 

five instalments of $10,000 each, or $50,000 in all-now overdue. No doubt the minister has a great deal to do, but it does seem to me a fair ground for respectful criticism that he is not in the position to tell us: "The fault does not lie with me. I have month by month inquired from the Department of Justice to whom I turned over the collection of this amount, and they tell me they have done such and such a thing." He ought to be able to tell us that a writ has been issued or the reason why a writ has not been issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think my hon.
friend is quite fair in that. I have repeatedly, through my deputy, asked how the matter stood with the Department of Justice. The department replied that they had the matter in hand, and they were corresponding with the firm, and so on. No later than this morning when my deputy was in my office I told him again to go personally and see the Justice Department, and find out if a writ had actually been served against the company. I did not forget the matter at all. We have been doing the very best that we could, and I am quite sure that my colleague the Minister of Justice is exercising his usual good judgment. You do not sue a responsible party right off. As a rule I understand that lawyers and the Justice Department first write to try and obtain a settlement, and if they fail they issue a writ.

I regret exceedingly, Sir, that the reputation of a firm in the city of St. John, apparently of very high standing in the opinion of the Minister of Marine as well as of the Minister of Customs, has been brought into question in this discussion, and it does seem to me that we should get some information in defence of this company. I do not happen to know the directorate of the St. John Rolling Mills Limited, but my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, who has been a resident of that city for many years, and is more or less intimately acquainted with local conditions, must, I am sure, have very good knowledge of the personnel of this company. I have no doubt that in the very strong efforts made by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine to collect this money he must have conferred not only with the Minister of Customs, but also with the Minister of Public Works in regard to this company, and those hon. gentlemen, who represent the Maritime Provinces in the Cabinet, no doubt, have general, if not in detail, information which would be of very great interest to this committee and would be of value to . the business reputation of the company in question; and, if I may be permitted to say so to my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, I think it is due to that company that he should give the committee such information in regard to it. If the company is composed of men of strong financial standing and acknowledged business integrity there can be no reason why my hon. friend should not disclose its personnel to this committee, as if they are men of that type the delay in payment would not amount to very much. But inasmuch as they have been in default since the first of January, 1921, the transaction naturally arouses suspicion in the minds of hon. gentlemen, particularly of those on this side of the House. So far as I know in a general way, the St. John Rolling Mills Company is a reputable business concern, and I would be very sorry to see it questioned without some very good

reason. The minister says he has a hard and fast contract with the firm, and it does seem to me there must be good grounds why they are not living up to the terms of that contract. He says that that contract was entered into openly and above-board. If that is so, I appeal to my hon. friend the Minister of Customs to inform the committee if he knows of any reason why this company is defaulting on that contract. I have no brief for the St. John Rolling Mills Company, but I do say that when the business methods of this or any other company are questioned in this House, and they have any defence to make, it should be given to the committee.
Carried.

There is perhaps a circumstance which makes it most imperative for both my hon. friends the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Customs to give this committee the fullest information possible concerning those tenders and the contract which was subsequently awarded^ There was an election in the city of St. John in September, 1920, and it is certainly a coincidence-at least some people may think it is a coincidence -that the contract was granted in such a peculiar way, that only part of the amount of the tender was accepted by the department; and that subsequently the company failed to meet the five instalments of the balance as they became due. I think under the circumstances my hon. friend's should give all the information they possibly can and put the matter fairly before the committee and before the country.
Carried.

I have a few remarks to make on this item, but I do not think it would be fair to mix the two questions as we have already mixed them somewhat to-night. There is, first, this contract for the sale of the Niobe and the submarines; and, second, the vote for the naval service proper. These two questions have been interwoven in such a way that confusion has resulted. I think we should clear up the sale of the Niobe first, but I ask that this item be not carried before we have a chance to express our views on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite right, the vote before the committee is for $2,500,000 for the naval service. While the sale of the Niobe has something to do with naval affairs, it has absolutely
[Mr. Copp.l
nothing to do with this vote. I am asking the committee to give their approval to the vote of $2,500,000, into which the Niobe does not enter at all. I will lay on the Table to-morrow all tenders and all the correspondence that we have had with this concern, and also a copy of the contract. I submit to hon. members that the sale of the Niobe has nothing whatever to do with this vote of $2,500,000.
The minister did not understand me rightly. He is asking for $2,500,000 for ships which have been accepted to replace the Niobe and we are perfectly in order in discussing the Niobe first.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me, I am not asking for $2,500,000 to purchase ships. I am asking for that amount to carry on the naval service of Canada, to maintain our docks at Halifax and Esquimalt, to maintain the naval college, and for the upkeep of our ships. It is quite in order to ask questions about the naval force when the vote is before the House, but the Niobe has nothing to do with this vote.

It is perfectly proper that we should deal with the Niobe transaction because this item covers the whole of the expenses of the department. The Chairman was asking whether the item should carry and I simply wanted to point out that I was refraining from offering any remarks on the naval service at this stage because I thought we might first clear up the Niobe deal.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that nothing in connection with the sale of the Niobe is involved in this item, and I would like a ruling whether the discussion with regard to the Niobe is in order.

With regard to the point of order, I submit that we are asked to vote an amount of $2,500,000 to provide for the maintenance of the Royal Canadian Navy, and that under it we are entitled to put all sorts of questions relating to the naval service. The Niobe is one of the ships that has been replaced by the new ships and we are entitled to know what has been done with the old ones, under what conditions they have been disposed of, and all details with regard to their sale. The sale of these ships involves an asset of the department, and that is connected with administration; therefore we are entitled to all information concerning them. Moreover, the question with regard to the Niobe was raised not by us, but by an hon.

gentleman on the other side, and very properly so; he deserves credit for bringing the matter to the attention of the committee. My contention is that if we are not satisfied with the administration of the naval service we are entitled to criticise this amount, and we would be justified in asking for a reduction of the vote if we thought the affairs of the department had not been properly conducted. I think the amount of the vote, $2,500,000 is quite sufficient to justify an inquiry on the part of members of! the committee into the whole administration of this service.
I would also point out that if this $100,000 had been received the minister would be asking now for a vote of $2,400,000 instead of $2,500,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, no.

I concur in the remarks of the hon. member for Three Rivers and the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier. Surely this House has the right to discuss a deal involving the sale of the Niobe to this firm. One very strong reason why we should be enabled to discuss it now is the fact that there is no other item in the Estimates under which the discussion could take place.

Speaking to the point of order, I submit that it surely is elementary that if a minister had so ill-managed the affairs of the Naval Department and that fact were clearly brought to light, it would have an important bearing on the intelligence of hon. members on this side as to how far they should vote any more money to be spent by a minister who is making these bad sales.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The point of order
has been raised by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) that the discussion of the sale of the cruiser Niobe is not in order on item 197, to provide for the maintenance of the Royal Canadian Navy, $2,500,000. During the time that I have occupied the Chair I have always endeavoured to keep the discussion strictly relevant to the item under consideration. I have, however, always observed the rule that all matters pertaining to all departments should be discussed in Committee of Supply if hon. members so desired, but that a discussion was out of order when there was in the Estimates another item upon which that discussion could with more relevancy and more propriety take place. I have looked over the Estimates and I find there is no item under which the sale
of the cruiser Niobe could be discussed so relevantly and so properly as under the present item. This is the only item in the Estimates concerning the administration and maintenance of the Royal Canadian Navy. The sale of a battleship belonging to the Dominion Government is certainly a matter which can be inquired into by this Committee, and I therefore rule that the discussion is in order.

I am not quite satisfied
that the Minister of Customs really wants to do such injustice to his friends as not to give this information to the Committee. From what has been said by the Minister of Marine, if this company is in such good financial standing as we hope it is and as I am bound to say I always understood it to be, it should meet its obligation under the contract. The Minister of Customs says in a general way that they are a firm of good financial standing in the community, and if that is so I cannot understand why they have defaulted in their payments. The Minister of Marine has made a very strong insinuation with regard to the business integrity of that firm, because he says that the only reason for their trying to get out of their contract is that the iron and brass and other materials in these vessels have fallen in price. Now, that is a statement made in this House, Mr. Chairman, and to my mind it affects very seriously the standing of that company. As I said a moment ago, I hold no brief for the company, but I do say that the minister should place before the committee any information he has in regard to the matter so that we may know just	how	to deal	with it.
If the company is strong and responsible financially, there is no reason that I can see why they should default upon their payments. They have defaulted now for five months and practically into six months. That is $60,000 that they are in default or will be in a few days under this contract. As I say, I have some pride in my province, and I regret exceedingly that the integrity, honesty and fair dealing of this company is brought into question by the very fact of the silence that has been practised by the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue (Mr. Wig-more), who, I am sure, as a business man and having done business in the city of St. John for many years, must have the information as regards this company. I again appeal to him, in defence of the honour of the corporation of the city that he represents and the province that we
4U3U

both represent, that he give to the committee that reasonable information upon which we can base an opinion in regard to this matter and see if we cannot shorten this debate and get along with the business as well as have the reputation of this corporation cleared up before this committee by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I do not see what
more I can say than I have said. I have stated before that, in my opinion, this company is thoroughly reliable. I know that the president or manager of this concern owns a good deal of property in St. John city.
Will my hon. friend give his name?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I gave the name before-H. J. Garson. I do not know what more information I can give. In my opinion this firm is absolutely solvent, and I do not know anything different from that. I have never gone into the bank to inquire into their financial condition, but I know that the president of this company owns a good deal of property in St. John city.
In his own name or in the name of the company?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: In his own name, and t know that the property which they own there, the New Brunswick Rolling Mills is a very valuable property. So far as I know, they own it. I have never made inquiry to find out whether there is anything against it or not. I am absolutely fair to the House when I make that statement..
Are the New Brunswick Rolling Mills still in operation?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: So far as I know they are still in operation. The last time I was in St. John was at the New Year. I know that things are quiet all over. I do not know the condition of the New Brunswick Rolling Mills at the present time, but I know they have been carrying on a very successful business during the past two or three years.

Has my hon. friend, being interested as a citizen of St. John and a member of the Government in getting this matter cleared up, had any communications, correspondence or personal interviews with this firm, during the course of this trouble that has been going on for five months, to see what reason there is for this company delaying payment?
FMr. Copp.]

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know of any reason why the company is delaying payment. Only, as I said before-the hon. gentleman was not in the House, I think, when I made the statement before-
I apologize then.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The only reason I
could give is the same reason why many other firms are trying to cancel their contracts not only in this business but in every other business, namely, because prices have dropped materially. I do not know of any other reason why they should not carry out their contract.
Does the minister base his opinion as to the solvency and reliability of this company upon the fact that the president owns in his own name in the city of St. John a good deal of valuable property? -

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I said besides that that the property that they have there in the situation in which it is, is very valuable at the present time even with the reduced value of real estate to-day. The property is on the line of the Canadian Pacific, and it is in a very valuable position in St. John as an industrial site off any kind.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: Will the minister off Marine and Fisheries let us have the information that the department. obtained from the mercantile marine agency before they made the contract with this company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am glad to tell my hon. friend that all the information which I could gather at the time was perfectly favourable in regard to the financial condition of the company. I have not said to-night, and I do not say now that this company is not financially good. Hon. gentlemen opposite are hinting and almost saying that the company is bankrupt; I have not said so.

One of the strongest
evidences of bankruptcy is failure to pay your bill. Any person who refuses to pay his honest debt cannot complain if somebody says that he is insolvent. The company must not be very sensitive on that point. Has the minister the Order in Council which was passed closing this transaction with this company? That might give us some information as to what took place in the transaction. I have never been a minister, and the strong possibilities are that I never shall be; but I understand that a minister putting through a contract reports to council the facts of

the case, and that an Order in Council is passed accepting the contract. Perhaps the minister could give us a copy of the report that he made to council on this transaction and the order that was passed at the time. That would be a very valuable record if the minister has it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will place on the table every tender that we got, the first, the second and the third time, all the correspondence that has taken place, a copy of the contract, a copy of the Order in Council. I shall be only too happy to do that. There is absolutely nothing Wrong with this transaction. And having promised to do that, and as we are all trying to prorogue at as early a date as possible, I hope hon. members will agree with me that, after spending two hours and 35 minutes on this and saying practically nothing at all about the vote of $2,500,000, perhaps we have spent a sufficient time on it. I will put all the information on the table to-morrow. I will do more than that; I will hold one of the items here, because after all, they are all Naval Service items. Therefore, hon. members will have every opportunity again after they have seen a copy of the contract, the Order in Council and the correspondence, to make any further remarks that they desire to make.
