The minister should allow this item to stand until he has the information, and then he will get through very quickly. He has been struggling with this thing for six months trying to make some advance in it; he has failed absolutely to get a dollar in six months, so that he must not complain of the little delay from now until to-morrow to get this information. He will get on very much better by saying that he will take up something else and let this item stand until this information is put in the possession of the committee.
The Chairman has decided that this is the only item on which this discussion can properly take place. '

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
That was the reason why he decided that it was in order on this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am not questioning the ruling of the Chair for a moment, but I should like to draw the Chairman's attention to the fact that all these items, 197, 198, 199, 200, 201, 202, 203, and 294 are Naval Service votes. Hon. members
have full right to ask any questions they like about the Niobe, Rainbow or anything else in regard to the Naval Service on any of these items, because they are all Naval Service items, as the appropriation shows.
I am sorry to differ from my hon. friend. The other items are not Naval Service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, they are.
Mr.	ARCHAMBAULT:	Item	198	is
hydrographic survey.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is Naval
Service.
Mr.	ARCHAMBAULT:	Item	199	is
fisheries protection service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is Naval
Service.
Mr.	ARCHAMBAULT:	Item	200	is
Radio-telegraphic service, and 201	is tidal
and current survey.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Those are Naval Service items.

The only item is 197. The only reason why the Chairman ruled that this discussion was in order was the fact that there was no other item in the Estimates on which this discussion could take place. Even if the hon. member will hold one item, it will not be in order to-morrow to discuss this special deal on that item.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: To show that I am not trying to shut off debate at all-I would like to make progress to-night-I will table all the information that has been asked for, and I want it understood now, if the Chairman will allow me, that hon. members have the right to discuss this question again. Let me point out to my hon. friend that I am on the Naval Service Estimates which amount to $3,726,980. They are all Naval Service Estimates. I would ask the Chair again if he does no# consider that all these Estimates are Naval Service Estimates; they are not fishery items nor marine items; they are Naval Service items.	.
I submit that even with the consent of the minister, the chairman could not allow the discussion of this matter on any other item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In previous sessions it has often occurred that an item has been allowed to stand in the Estimates of one of the ministers with the understanding that any subject concerning his de-

partment could be discussed upon that particular item. I am sure that by unanimous consent this discussion could be resumed upon some other item, if the committee now wishes this item to pass and to proceed to other items.
Did I understand you to say, Mr. Chairman, that it would require unanimous consent to discuss this matter on some other item at a later date?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Strictly speaking, it would require unanimous consent, but if the hon. members of the Opposition desire to discuss a matter, and the minister in charge of the Estimates desires to allow the discussion, unanimous consent is generally given.

It is not a
matter of certainty.
We could let this item stand until we get the papers, and take up the other items, leaving this one open for further discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That would be the best way out of the difficulty. Another way would be to obtain the unanimous consent of the committee now that on a certain item to be specified by the hon. minister, this discussion would be in order at a later date.

It is very questionable whether this committee or Parliament can bind itself in advance as to what it is going to do, and particularly bind members who are not now present. Members are absent from both sides of the House, and I am not so sure that we could make such a ruling, outside of an Act of Parliament itself, that would be binding upon them.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is not going to get off as easily as he thinks. He is practically a new man in the House, and every minister before he is very long in harness learns that the less he says in putting through his Estimates, and the closer he keeps to the item under discussion, the better off he is. The minister to-night swung off into a full discussion of the naval policy, and told us of the sins of omission and commission of both parties for the last fifteen years. He is not going to escape after his fling at this side of the House to-night without hearing something about it.
The hon. minister was not in the House in 1909 when the naval policy of Canada was first discussed, but if he will look up

the discussion in Hansard of March 30, 1909, he will see that hon. gentlemen now sitting around him who were in the House at that time voted unanimously with us on this side in favour of the Laurier naval policy. There was not a single dissenting voice to that resolution. The Laurier policy received the full and ample support of every man in the House. Now the minister comes here to-night, twelve or more years later, and taunts us about the Laurier naval policy. The Laurier naval policy had its basis in the resolution moved by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, then the Hon. George E. Foster. The Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was then leader of the Government, accepted his resolution with very slight changes and with those very slight changes the whole Parliament accepted the resolution upon which was based the Naval Act of 1910. If my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries wants to resurrect the question of the conduct of his party and the reasons for their rightabout face in connection with the naval policy of Canada, I shall have no hesitation at all in discussing that matter with ' him. The naval policy was all right at that time, but in the early part of 1910, I think, an election was held in Drum-mond-Arthabasca, in the province of Quebec. It was found that the naval policy of Laurier which has been agreed to by every man in this House, was not popular with some people in the province of Quebec, so at once there was a volte-face by hon. gentlemen opposite, and they at once threw to the winds the naval policy of Laurier which they had supported. When the right hon. gentleman who is now Minister of Trade and Commerce was asked by some gentlemen in Quebec: What shall we do in this election? Shall we vote for those who are opposing the policy for the defence of Canada and the defence of Great Britain? Shall we vote against that policy? What did the right hon. gentleman then say? What does it matter whether they are refusing to do anything for Great Britain or not? Anything to beat Laurier. That was the policy of the gentlemen amongst whom my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries now takes refuge, and upon whose company he prides himself. At that time it suited him better, perhaps, to be with us supporting the Laurier policy. I say that the hon. gentleman has no business, just because he happens to renege from his party and take shelter with the party opposite,

to taunt us because we were with him in supporting the policy of that time. He ought at least to have modesty enough to say nothing about the policy that he was supporting himself then. I think it ill becomes any man-I care not who he is- who, after supporting a certain policy at one time, leaves his party for some reason or other to befoul those who were formerly with him on the policy which he supported. There is nothing at all to be proud of in this matter. The hon: gentleman says that they have a new navy and a new policy. I want to ask the Conservative party when, where, and on what occasion they agreed upon a new naval policy? There is not a single man of independent standing on the Government side who is in favour of this naval policy. The main body of their support, they say, they have from Ontario. I tell them on my responsibility that there is no enthusiasm in Ontario or among Ontario members in regard to this new navy. In the first sitting of the Borden Administration in 1912 the then Minister of Naval Affairs, Mr. Hazen, shortly after he came into the House, in a speech declared that the naval policy of the Laurier Administration was abandoned once for all; it was not the policy of the Borden Government. He said they had no policy, that they were going to England the next year, and after a consultation on the other side the Government would announce their policy. Any one who reads Mr. Hazen's speech on that occasion will find that statement therein contained. Their next declaration was this, that we could not build ships on this side. They said it would take fifty years to build anything worth mentioning; that is what the leader of the Government at that time informed us. They decided to abandon any naval policy and to take $35,000,000 and purchase some ships from the Old Country and bring them over here in the name of Canada. That was their policy. It was defeated in the Senate after it had been forced through the House under closure, and we heard nothing whatever about the policy until to-night when the minister informs us we have a brand-new navy and naval policy, and that we have wiped out the old naval policy of the Laurier Administration. There is absolutely no foundation for such a statement. The matter was never submitted to the people, as was promised, and that being the case the minister has no mandate to have these vessels in his possession; nor have we the right to vote this money if we have any regard for the wishes of the people. There
was no question of this kind before the people in 1917. The people, in fact, took it for granted that the Laurier policy had been abandoned by this Government, and they had every reason to suppose that they would be consulted on any question of a navy before any particular policy was adopted. The Government did not submit the matter to them in 1917, and the people to-day have the right to suppose that we are not going to invest in any naval affairs or launch on any permanent policy until the matter is pronounced upon by them. This discussion has been precipitated to-night by the minister's taunting us with having had a false navy policy. Well, whatever our policy might have been, it was concurred in absolutely and completely by both sides of the House. If it was a good policy we are all entitled to credit for it, and if it was bad we are all equally responsible, and we must not find very much fault with the Rolling Mills of St. John for not standing by their word if the part of Parliament composed of hon. gentlemen opposite have not enough respect for the resolution they passed in 1909 to abide by the consequences of that resolution. Everything in connection with this navy should be thoroughly investigated, and this matter should not pass until we have some information in regard to the way the business of the department is carried on. It will not impose any hardship on the minister to let this item stand. He could go on with other items and get the necessary information in regard to this matter in the meantime. I do say, with more or less feeling, that I deprecate the idea of the minister launching upon a tirade practical abuse of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, their policy and their leaders. The policy which he is now so vigorously advocating is one for which he has no authority from the people; he had no mandate from the people to receive this gift. The vessels were only in the way in the Old Country; they did not know where to put them and threw them off their hands upon the minister, so that we should have the large expense in connection with them. No doubt the minister is in full sympathy with them in having vessels which they do not know what to do with. He can appreciate their position when he himself has sixty-five or seventy such craft which he is crowding into every mill pond in every part of the country so long as he can get them out of sight. On that principle, no doubt, he is willing to go to the assistance of those who have

such ships as they cannot dispose of. We have no use for these ships that have been given us. I hope they will never be used, and I cannot see why we should expend money in connection with them that can and ought to be spent to better purpose. I do not think that the minister can defend a policy of spending money just for the glory of having a navy for which we have no use.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As we have spent three hours now discussing the sale of the Niobe, and in order to give hon. members all the information that they ask for by tabling the facts, as I have promised to do to-morrow, I move that further consideration of this item be postponed, and I hope that hon. members will allow the other items to pass as we come to them.

Motion agreed to.
Item stands.
Fisheries Protection Service and to provide for the repairs and maintenance of the Fishery-protection steamers, $370,000.
What provisions are made for coastal protection in the Maritime Provinces this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have two fishery protection vessels in service in the Maritime Provinces and also two which are laid up. We have not sufficient money to keep the four in commission.

Item agreed to.
Pay of temporary officers and clerks at Headquarters, at Halifax and Esquimau Dockyards, $40,000.

How long will these
employees be needed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The item of $40,000 is for the pay of temporary officers and clerks at headquarters, Halifax and Esquimalt dock yards. The work is just of a temporary nature.

That is what the item
says. I want to know how long they will be there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is a pretty
hard question to answer; it is difficult to say how long they will be there. We do not intend to keep them any longer than is absolutely necessary.

The time they will be
kept will be proportionate to their usefulness. How long will they be useful, and what are they doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The permanent
organization of the department is based on

minimum requirements, and makes no allowance for emergencies, temporary pressure of work, unforeseen absence through illness or other causes, et cetera. The sum provided under this head is for the purpose of meeting such emergencies.

I do not want to detain
the Committee but I would like to ascertain the exact services of these officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They are doing
what ever work the permanent employees do. They may be sometimes employed at clerical work and sometimes at other work. As I say, we are asking this vote to employ these men in a temporary capacity until such times as the Civil Service Commission give us the necessary permanent staff.

Item agreed to.
Fisheries: To provide for salaries, construction and maintenance of fish breeding establishments, $365,000.	[DOT]

I am
chiefly concerned with the lobster hatcheries which have been abandoned by the department, and I want to know what the minister has done in the direction of substituting something in their place. I am told that on the Atlantic coast where those lobster hatcheries were, we are back now pretty much to the old method of catching the seed lobster and boiling it in the pot, and losing the seed. That is what I feared would happen when the minister undertook to abolish the system that had been in operation for a number of years. The minister will remember that his predecessors had established a large number of these hatcheries on the coast, but that-on the advice given him by some theorist in the city of Kingston, some professor who learnt his knowledge of fish out of a book

the minister, without consulting the House, or telling the members from the Maritime Provinces anything about it, closed the hatcheries all along the coast and sold them, and destroyed the system that had been built up in the course of many years. I would like to know if the minister has any information to give us as to what he proposes to do in the future in regard to that branch of the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member, I think, is aware that the reason
12 p.m. we closed these lobster hatcheries was because it was in the interest of the greater production of lobsters. Under the hatchery system the production of young fry was only about 30 per cent as compared with 100 per cent in the natural way when the female lobster

extrudes her eggs. Therefore in the interest of the lobster industry, and especially as lobsters were becoming more and more scarce, we sold those old lobster hatcheries. But we have improved the regulations. We have expert men going down through those districts lecturing to the fishermen, and we are doing everything we can for the better care of the lobster industry and to secure greater production as well.

If the
argument of' the minister is any good it would apply to other fish as well as lobsters. He is carrying on the breeding of fish of various kinds on the coast and he is asking us to vote large sums of money for that purpose. If his argument that the lobster can be better propagated in the natural way than by any other method is a good one it applies equally to trout, bass, or any of the other varieties of fish that he is propagating. I think he will find it difficult to maintain such an argument. Instead of 30 per cent production of lobsters I question if we are getting any percentage of production at all. The minister apparently is not familiar with the history of this branch of the service. The experience at first was that these seed lobsters were destroyed: they were caught by the fishermen, thrown into the basket with the others, put into the pot in the factories and boiled. The hatcheries were built for the purpose of saving those lobsters that happened to be caught in that way. Inducements were offered to the fishermen to save the seed. That seed went into the hatchery and my hon. friend admits 30 per cent of lobsters were rescued. At present I am told that none are rescued, so that 30 per cent was better than nothing. I would like if my hon. friend could give me any proof that he is getting even a 30 per cent production out of the lobsters that are caught in the traps with seed on them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not pose as an authority on lobsters or fish generally. I can only give the advice tendered by scientific men, who have informed me that lobster eggs are fertilized and that the female lobster really hatches each one. Therefore, the propagation is very much larger in the natural way when the lobster is free.

But
are not those female lobsters caught?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have carried on a propaganda for some years to prevail upon fishermen not to catch these small female lobsters, and when they do
catch them to put them hack in the sea again.

Has
my hon. friend sold all the lobster hatcheries on the coast? I understood there were about thirty.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, they are all sold.
Has the hatchery at Buctouche in the county of Kent been sold? If so, to whom and for what amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I find I was incorrect in that statement. They are all sold but two, and one of those two is the Buctouche hatchery,
Where is the other one?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am sorry I
cannot tell just where the other lobster hatchery is located that is not sold.

How
much has been received for those hatcheries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Canso, $1,750;
Shippigan, $610; House harbour, $760; Port Daniel, $775; Arichat, $1,000; Little Bras d'Or, $1,605; Georgetown, $555; Charlottetown, $700; Bay View, $650; Shemogue, $150; Antigonish, $635; Inverness, $350.50.
The minister made reference to the results of the investigation by scientists of this question. Were these scientists unanimous?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I believe so.

My information is
that one of the head scientists of his own department, Professor Prince, did not endorse the policy of the Government in disposing of these hatcheries. If that is so, I do not quite agree with the minister that the question was decided correctly. Professor Prince was brought to this country many years ago, and he made a particular study of our lobsters. According to my information he opposed this policy of the Government, but I understand a few professors gathered themselves down by the seashore for a few months-enjoying themselves no doubt-and decided this question as against a man who had studied the question in the Old Country and had twenty years' experience. The first lobster hatchery established in this country was in 1896 at Pictou, and my information is that the particular zone supplied by the fry from

that hatchery maintained a supply of lobsters much larger than those in any other zone along the coast of Prince Edward Island and around Pictou. This would go a long way to convince me that those hatcheries were doing good work, and that the only thing necessary was careful administration of each hatchery and giving the experiment time to prove itself. There were many features connected with the operation of those hatcheries which in my judgment did not contribute to good results, but rather to the very destruction of the lobsters. I would suggest that if the thirty per cent of fry gathered in the hatcheries was preserved, that is a much larger percentage than is preserved now under natural conditions. The fry of lobsters is subject to great destruction in its early stages, and that was the main reason for establishing these hatcheries. My belief is that they will yet be reopened at a much greater cost than the minister has received at this sale. These hatcheries were closed and sold over-night. In fact, they were sold in such a way as to indicate that the minister was eager to get clear of them, just as in the same department they closed up some of the life-saving stations overnight.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The biological
board unanimously recommended that we close up these hatcheries, and Professor Prince as a member of that board concurred in its decision and also with the report that Professor Knight made. I can only go by the advice of our scientific officers. With regard to the sale of the hatcheries, we called for public tenders, and it has taken us almost two years to sell them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This matter was brought before the Standing Committee of this House on Fisheries and was very thoroughly discussed so that I did not by any means close the hatcheries, simply on information that I got from the scientific officers. They were not sold for a year, and the matter was thoroughly gone into by this committee. I wish to point out also that before we closed the hatcheries and changed the regulations it was not illegal for fishermen to catch the small female lobsters and take them to the canneries where the eggs were brushed off. It is now illegal to do that, and we have taken many important and useful steps by our regulations to improve materially the conditions of the lobster industry. From information I have received from the practical as well as the scientific officers of the department and from hon. members of the House,
I.am satisfied that this is the case.

I do
not like to contradict the minister, but I have attended the meetings of the Fisheries Committee ever since I have been a member of this House and I have never heard that the question of the closing of the lobster

hatcheries was submitted to that committee. It is news to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I want to make
it quite clear to my hon. friend: I did not submit to the committee the question of the closing of the hatcheries. I said that the department decided on the advice of practical and scientific men that it would be wise to close them, but before selling them the matter was thoroughly discussed before the Standing Committee of the House on Fisheries and the hatcheries were not sold until a year after they were closed.

Some
of them were sold and a protest was entered by members, including myself, to which the minister paid no attention. Of course, the fact that we were protesting as I am doing to-night did not affect the matter. The minister did not make any further investigation; he accepted the advice of the men whom he calls the scientific gentlemen. The minister is not able to show by the reports of his officers along the coast that he is saving the lobsters that were being utilized in the hatcheries. At least, he is not giving us any evidence to that effect; my information is that they are not being saved.

I would ask the minister
not to dispose of the Buctouche hatchery at least for a year or so. Many of the people on the shore believe that it is useful, and if it is decided not to close it up the same hatchery might be used for future operations.

Item agreed to.
Ocean and river service

to provide for the temporary relief of distressed seamen and to cover the expenses of shipping forms-further amount required, $3,500.

The minister is no
doubt aware that the marine hospital at Louisburg has been closed. May I have the minister's attention? Perhaps he is not sufficiently interested in the seamen to listen to a member when he is putting his case. If he is not, I will prefer the matter on some future occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I was listening
to my hon. friend. About two years ago the matters affecting sick mariners were transferred to the Department of Health. This item is to provide for the temporary relief of distressed seamen-to bring to their home ports those who may be wrecked.

With respect to this
hospital in Louisburg, I happened to be before another minister of the Government yesterday with respect to hospitals and he assured me that one of the remedies for my difficulty was that there was a hospital at Louisburg.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am sorry, but
I do not know anything about the marine hospitals; they come under my colleague, the Minister of Health.

Can the minister tell us
how much was transferred from the Marine Department to the Health Department arising out of the sick mariner's benefit fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The moneys derived by
way of levy for this purpose form part of the general revenue; they do not constitute a special fund.

Quite a number of hospitals in the seaport towns were supported to some extent by the Marine Department out of this fund-that is, certain beds were maintained in those hospitals for sick mariners. Many of the hospitals have complained that the per diem allowance for these beds is not sufficient. Last year we tried to get a further allowance on that account, for St. John, but it was just at the time that this transfer was being made. I then maintained that if there was a large fund which had been collected by way of mariners' dues at least the interest should be devoted to the payment of a larger per diem allowance in these hospitals in order to give the sailors better accommodation. In St. John the accommodation is not sufficient to take care of sick mariners who are there in the winter season. In fact, in a great many cases the people of St. John are unable to get into the public hospital. A larger wing or something of that sort should be built to take care of these sick mariners, and the same applies to the other ports in the Maritime Provinces where contributions to this fund are rather large. I should like to bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Health (Mr. Calder), to whom this matter has now been transferred.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I assume the whole discussion is out of order; but I might state that the revenues derived from the Maritime Provinces this year are not as large as the expenditures, and I doubt very much if there is any fund such as that to which my hon. friend refers.
Item agreed to.
Lighthouse and coast service-signal service -further amount required, $4,000.

I have heard complaints made about the absence of telephones in lighthouses. I think I once made some inquiries of the department, and I was informed that it was not considered to be good policy that telephones should be supplied to light keepers. I have here, if the House will bear with me for a minute, an extract from a newspaper which seems to illustrate the need for telephones from lighthouses to the mainland. This is from an item in the Shelburne Gazette of a few days ago:	.
Messrs. Robert D. McKay and Frank Owen, of this town, had an exciting experience on Saturday last while fishing between Gray's Island and Gull Rock.
Their motor boat refused to go and for sometime they were pitched about in lively style by the waves which were big enough to make life in an unmanageable motor boat anything but pleasant. Fortunately they were seen by Beaumont Decker, keeper of the Light on McNutt's Island, who walked between two and three miles to give the alarm. Two boats put off to rescue of the two fishermen, one containing Sydney Slate and the other Stanford Kenney and Freeman Atwood and it was not long before the men were towed to terra firma.
They lost their dory and a tub of trawl and had an experience they do not wish to have repeated.
This was a case in which there was danger; the lightkeeper saw the danger, but he had to walk two miles in order to give an alarm. That is an illustration of the fact that lightkeepers should be provided with telephones. Would the minister give consideration to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall be glad to give every consideration to the suggestion of my hon. friend. We have not the money this year; but it is a matter that should receive attention, and as soon as the finances of the country will permit, I hope we may have telephones, at least in some of the most important stations.

Item agreed to.
Fisheries-to provide for the expenses of counsel in the Quebec fisheries reference before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, $21,645.55.
Can the minister give us any idea what is the result of the decision of the Privy Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Privy Council a few months ago gave a decision under which we are now acting, namely that
fisheries in navigable streams leading from the sea were no longer vested in Provincial Governments, but were under the Federal Government. Therefore, we have notified the Provincial Government at Quebec that all these fisheries in navigable streams leading from the sea now come under the Federal authorities, and all those that were not licensees must apply to the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

Item agreed to.
Ottawa Parliament buildings-restoration,
$1,000,000. [DOT]

speechtext:

Mr. MeCURDY: One or two members wish to discuss this item further, and it had better stand.

I would suggest to the minister that when he brings this item on again, it would be well for him if possible to have the original contract with the contractor and the contract with the architect. We would like to know what those contracts are, particularly the one with the architect, and when the terms of the first contract became exhausted, what was the nature of the second arrangement that was made under which the architect is getting paid now.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that a message has been received from the Senate acquainting this House that the Senate hath agreed to a free conference desired with the Senate for the purpose of communicating the reasons which induced the Commons not to concur in the amendments made by the Senate to the Bill No. 60, intituled: "An Act to [DOT]hmend the Judges Act," and hath appointed the Honourable Messieurs Bennett, Bostock, Lougheed (Sir James), Ross (Middleton), and Thompson as managers on their part of the said conference, and also that the managers of the Free Conference on the part of the Senate will meet in the Senate Committee Room No. 262, at 10.30 o'clock in the morning, on the thirtieth day of May instant.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Ballantyne the House adjourned at 12.35 a.m.
